12 Deep Learning-Based Ultrasound Analysis Using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) Methods for Breast Cancer

P. Manju Bala
S. Usharani
A. Balachandar
R. Rajmohan

Abstract

Medical imaging is one of the most crucial components of breast cancer screening. Ultrasound is notable for its noninvasive methodology and exceptional sensitivity. However, interpretability issues with deep learning models make them unsuitable for application in therapeutic contexts. To diagnose breast cancer, this study proposes to combine deep learning-based ultrasound analysis with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methodologies. This chapter examines several XAI methods, including model explanations, saliency maps, and attention processes. It illustrates how these methods may be used to make deep learning models’ decision-making processes more transparent. Improving the comprehensibility and offering valuable information about the predictions made by automated diagnostic systems will assist physicians in better understanding and placing confidence in these systems. The accurate diagnosis of breast cancer can be improved by combining deep learning technology with XAI. We verify this by conducting thorough testing on ultrasound data. By using these techniques, the quality of clinical judgments and patient treatment for breast cancer may be improved.

Keywords: Deep learning, ultrasound analysis, breast cancer, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), interpretability, diagnostic imaging,

12.1 Introduction

The most common and possibly lethal disease affecting women worldwide is breast cancer. Accurate and timely diagnosis is essential for better patient outcomes and lowering death rates. Because ultrasonography is noninvasive and very sensitive, it is an essential tool for the diagnosis and characterization of breast lesions. The identification of complex patterns in diagnostic pictures has been made easier by these cutting-edge algorithms [1]. Research on clinical solicitations has advanced considerably as an effect of the capacity to match and occasionally exceed the diagnostic precision of human specialists. However, the opaque, “black box” character of these complex technologies can occasionally mask their real effectiveness. The absence of clearness has led to grave anxieties nearly the legitimacy and reliability, particularly in the dangerous medical field [2]. A significant development in response to the increasing need for directness and dependability in AI-powered structures is explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). The goal of XAI was to unveil the underlying mechanisms of artificial intelligence models and offer significant perceptions into their decision-making processes. This clearness was practical as well as ethically crucial, particularly in medical settings where vital choices are frequently made based on the guidelines provided by such rules. The lack of transparency has generated significant concerns over their dependability and acceptance, particularly within the high-risk field of healthcare [3]. XAI has emerged as a key technology to meet the growing demand for reliability and limpidity in AI-driven systems [4]. The goal of XAI was to clarify the internal mechanisms of AI models and offer important visions into how they make decisions. This transparency was important from both a practical and moral standpoint, especially in scientific settings where important choices frequently depended on the direction these systems provided [5].

Deep learning techniques have become powerful tools for automating the examination of medical images in recent years [6]. These provide the possibility of increased precision and effectiveness in diagnosis. A type of deep learning model called “convolutional neural networks” (CNNs) has demonstrated remarkable performance in a variety of medical imaging applications, including the analysis of breast ultrasound images [7]. Nevertheless, the opaque nature of these black boxes presents obstacles in understanding the decision-making process, hence restricting their practicality and acceptance in clinical settings. To solve this issue, XAI techniques deliver insights into the deep learning models’ decision-making processes [8]. By clarifying the variables and patterns utilized for predictions, XAI techniques improve interpretability and foster confidence between end users and clinicians. The term XAI describes how readily people can understand and recognize a model’s operation. It has garnered significant attention in recent years. An explanation of a model seeks to offer detailed insights on how a machine learning model is created, illuminate the reasons behind its accuracy, and improve reliability in the model’s predictions. Therefore, the use of machine learning improves the machine learning models’ transparency, interpretability, fairness, robustness, privacy, trust, and dependability. A number of approaches have been suggested and used recently to improve machine learning model comprehension [9]. There are several taxonomies available to describe machine learning. Consumers can request certain sorts of information or go further into an interactive explanation until they are satisfied, but a static explanation doesn’t alter based on feedback from consumers. While a local explanation is specific to a single prediction, a global explanation considers the behavior of the entire model. A post hoc explanation necessitates the application of an extra technique to explain a model after it has been trained, whereas an instantaneously interpretable model is one that is transparent by nature and understandable to the majority of users [10]. Self-explanatory does not always imply immediately clear. It generates local explanations on its own. While a model’s representation may highlight particular features and not be a full model in and of itself, a surrogate model is usually a more simple and intelligible form that approximates a more sophisticated model.

This work provides a thorough examination of deep learning-based ultrasound analysis for the identification and categorization of breast cancer [11]. We point out the challenges associated with understanding deep learning techniques in medical imaging and discuss the necessity of employing XAI techniques to overcome these challenges. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive examination of various XAI tactics, including saliency maps, attentional mechanisms, and model explanations. We emphasize their relevance in the specific setting of breast ultrasonography assessment. Furthermore, we discuss the advantages of XAI’s capabilities in enhancing the precision of diagnoses, assisting in scientific decision-making, and eventually improving results for persons impacted by breast cancer diagnosis and treatment [12]. Our objective is to bridge the gap between AI-powered automated analysis and medical practice by merging deep learning with XAI. This will enhance trust, transparency, and effectiveness in breast ultrasound imaging.

12.2 Related Works

A number of studies have looked at the analysis of breast ultrasonography using deep learning techniques. Particularly, these studies have focused on recognizing anomalies, classifying them, breaking them down, and assessing the risk involved. A highly developed deep learning model created especially for the purpose of recognizing breast lesions in ultrasound images was presented by Peta et al. [13]. The framework demonstrated impressive performance in terms of both sensitivity and specificity created a deep learning system to segment breast tumors in ultrasound images [14]. Their system outperformed traditional methods, showing better performance. Furthermore, researchers have explored how to apply ensemble approaches and transfer learning to improve the deep learning models’ capacity to forecast accurately and handle data variances in breast ultrasonography analysis. Transfer learning from pretrained CNN models was used to enhance the classification of breast lesions in ultrasound images [15]. Furthermore, Gulum et al. [16] proposed an ensemble learning approach that combines several deep learning models to increase breast cancer diagnostic accuracy. Although deep learning algorithms have demonstrated encouraging results in the analysis of breast ultrasonography, their interpretability problems remain a major obstacle. Researchers are attempting to combine deep learning-based ultrasonic research with XAI techniques to overcome this problem. A weighted class of gradient stimulation representation is a technique that Chaddad et al. [17] suggested to visually highlight regions of interest in ultrasound images and provide explanations for model predictions.

The use of attention processes and model explanations to enhance the interpretability of deep learning techniques for breast ultrasonography analysis has been the subject of recent study [18]. For the purpose of classifying breast lesions, proposed an attention-guided deep learning model [19]. This approach focuses on and highlights the regions that are useful in ultrasound images. Furthermore, a system that makes use of gradient-based attribution techniques was developed by Di Miranda [20] to generate clear and concise explanations for deep learning-based breast cancer diagnosis. Explainable multiclass classification for breast cancer subtyping is the main topic of the study [21]. It introduces a method that combines integrative feature selection techniques with explainable AI to improve classification performance. The approach aims to enhance interpretability and transparency in the classification process, particularly for complex multi-class problems like breast cancer subtyping. The DNN [22] is trained to generate textual descriptions of ultrasound images, providing clinicians with informative summaries that aid in diagnosis and interpretation. By improving communication between radiologists and other medical specialists, this strategy promotes more efficient teamwork and decision-making in the detection and treatment of breast cancer. According to Ellenrieder et al. [23], incorporating XAI into radiology education fosters a deeper knowledge of AI-based diagnostic procedures among radiologists, which improves learning outcomes and increases diagnostic accuracy.

12.3 Methods and Materials

12.3.1 Description of Data

The dataset used for evaluation and training comprises a specific number of ultrasound images. It also includes patient demographics and detailed annotations, such as lesion boundaries and pathology results. This indicates the specific preprocessing techniques employed on the dataset, such as normalization, augmentation, or data manipulation. The dataset utilized in this study consists of a compilation of breast ultrasound images acquired from various medical institutions and sources. The ultrasound images are obtained using conventional clinical ultrasound equipment that has different transducer frequencies and imaging settings. The dataset consists of a varied assortment of breast ultrasound images obtained from credible medical institutes and sources. The images are obtained using conventional ultrasound machines that have transducers with frequencies ranging from 5 to 15 MHz. These devices can capture both B-mode and Doppler imaging techniques. The dataset comprises images acquired from patients undergoing a range of breast ultrasonography tests, encompassing screening, diagnostic assessment, and subsequent procedures for monitoring.

The annotations in the dataset are methodically conducted by skilled radiologists or clinicians. Annotations commonly entail defining regions of interest (ROIs) that correlate to breast lesions, if they exist. The annotations may consist of bounding boxes or segmentation masks that delineate the boundaries of suspicious lesions. They are accompanied by pathology data that indicate the type of the lesion, such as whether it is benign or malignant. The ground truth annotations undergo thorough verification by consensus readings and histological confirmation if possible, guaranteeing the dataset’s trustworthiness and accuracy. As a way to confirm the integrity and accuracy of the data, the dataset is subjected to meticulous preparation. Preprocessing includes activities such as resizing images, normalizing them, and removing artifacts. Furthermore, augmentation approaches are utilized to improve the variety of the dataset and strengthen the resilience of the method. Augmentation techniques encompass various picture transformations such as rotation, scaling, flipping, and translation. In addition, techniques are employed to tackle the disparity in class distribution, specifically between benign and malignant lesions, to achieve a balanced representation in the dataset. The use example is effectively divided into training, validation, and test sets to aid in model building, hyperparameter tweaking, and performance evaluation. Usually, between 70% and 80% of the dataset is allocated to the training set, which is the set that receives the most attention. The test sets and validation sets then share the remaining amount. Apart from offering discrete datasets for verification and evaluation, this division guarantees that the technique is instructed on an extensive and varied use sample. Patient demographics like age, gender, and relevant clinical history may be included in the dataset. Stringent protocols are implemented to guarantee the privacy and confidentiality of patients, whereby all data is rendered anonymous and stripped of identifying information in accordance with ethical principles and legislation. Approval from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) and informed consent are acquired as required to maintain ethical standards in the utilization of data for research objectives. Figure 12.1 describes the process of the dataset.

12.3.1.1 Image Acquisition

The ultrasonic images are obtained utilizing transducers with frequencies ranging from 5 to 15 MHz, which may capture both B-mode and Doppler imaging techniques. Images are acquired from patients who are undergoing breast ultrasound tests for several purposes, such as screening, diagnostic assessment, and follow-up. During the acquisition of ultrasound pictures from the dataset, careful measures are taken to guarantee the quality, relevance, and integrity of the data for future analysis. At first, photos are chosen according to predetermined criteria that are relevant to the goals of the study. These criteria include information about the patients, their clinical conditions, and the features of the lesions. The dataset is used to extract and arrange photos that fulfill specific criteria. These images are organized in standardized formats to ensure compatibility across different imaging equipment. Then, preprocessing techniques, including scaling, normalization, and artifact removal, are used to enhance the consistency and quality of the images. In addition, the annotations linked to the chosen photos are thoroughly examined to confirm their veracity, usually by means of expert evaluations and histopathology reports. Quality control techniques are employed to rectify any flaws detected throughout the acquisition process, guaranteeing that the dataset upholds elevated levels of integrity. Then, to guarantee fair representation of various diseases and imaging settings, the dataset is divided into test, validation, and training sets. The utmost importance is placed on ethical considerations, and rigorous steps are implemented to protect patient privacy and adhere to ethical rules and legislation. By using this thorough picture capture approach, researchers may guarantee the dependability and ethical soundness of the dataset, establishing a strong basis for later analysis and model building.

12.3.1.2 Annotation and Ground Truth

Experienced radiologists or clinicians mark each ultrasound image in the dataset to outline ROIs that correlate to breast lesions, if they are present. Annotations encompass bounding boxes or segmentation masks that delineate the perimeters of suspicious lesions, along with corresponding pathology findings (e.g., benign or malignant). The accuracy of the ground truth annotations is ensured by conducting consensus readings and, whenever possible, confirming them through histological examination.

12.3.1.3 Data Preparation

Data preparation is an essential phase in making ultrasonic pictures for exploration using deep learning techniques. It guarantees that the data is of excellent quality and appropriate for model training. An essential preprocessing step is picture normalization, which seeks to standardize the intensity values of pixels across images. The mathematical expression for this procedure is

Normalized Image = Original Image − Mean/Standard Deviation

where the mean and standard deviation are calculated using the complete dataset. Normalization aids in reducing fluctuations in picture intensity levels, facilitating more consistent and effective model convergence during the training process. Additionally, data intensification methods like rotation and flipping are used to increase the resilience of the model and improve the diversity of the dataset. In mathematical terms, augmentation refers to the process of modifying the initial picture I by applying transformation matrices T:

Iaugmented = T.I

These modifications mimic changes to imaging conditions and improve the model’s ability to generalize to new data. Furthermore, synthetic minority oversampling techniques, or fake data production systems, can be used to address unbalanced datasets that include underrepresented classes. SMOTE creates artificial samples for the underrepresented class by interpolating between adjacent examples. From a mathematical perspective, this can be expressed as

Synthetic Sample = Random (sample1,sample2)

where Sample1 and Sample2 are randomly chosen cases from the minority class. By undergoing these preprocessing procedures, ultrasound pictures are converted into a refined, equitable, and standardized dataset, establishing the foundation for efficient deep learning model training and precise breast cancer detection.

12.3.1.4 Dataset Splitting

The dataset is divided into training, validation, and test sets to make model building, hyperparameter adjustment, and performance evaluation easier. Usually, the training phase of the dataset is assigned a larger percentage (about 70–80%), while the remaining part is divided equally between validation and testing (around 10–15% each). Mathematically, the process of splitting a dataset can be expressed as follows:

Let O denote the original dataset containing M samples, signified as O = {(xi, yi)}Mi=1, where xi is the input, i.e., an ultrasound image, and yi is the equivalent label (e.g., benign or malignant).

There are three subsets within the dataset.

Training Set (Otrain):

  • Typically, the majority of the dataset is allocated to the training set to facilitate model learning. Let Mtrain indicate how many samples there are in the training set. Mathematically, one way to visualize the training set is as (Otrain) = {(xi,yi)}Mtraini=1.

Validation Set (Oval):

  • To assist in overfitting, the validation set is used to calculate the performance of the method and adjust hyperparameters in training. Let Mval denote the number of trials in the validation set.

  • The validation set may be expressed mathematically as (Oval) = {(xi,yi) }Mvali=1.

Test Set (Otest):

  • The test set is reserved for the final analysis of the trained model’s effectiveness, offering a dispassionate appraisal of its capacity for generalization. Let Mtest be the sample count in the test set.

  • The test set may be expressed mathematically as (Otest) = {(xi,yi)}Mtesti=1.

12.3.1.5 Dataset Characteristics

The collection consists of diverse ultrasound images that depict several breast diseases, such as benign tumors, malignant lesions, cysts, fibroadenomas, and other anomalies. To enable subgroup analysis and risk stratification, patient demographics such as age, gender, and clinical history may be provided. The dataset may encompass various imaging methods, equipment manufacturers, and common imaging artifacts found in clinical practice. A wide range of characteristics is included in the dataset chosen for deep learning-based ultrasound analysis for breast cancer detection, all of which are essential for the careful building and exacting assessment of the model. Because there are a lot of ultrasound pictures in the dataset, there is enough information for training, validation, and testing. This ensures that the produced models are strong and can be applied to many situations. The dataset is carefully annotated by qualified radiologists or doctors, ensuring that the annotations are of high quality. The annotations are validated using consensus readings and histological confirmation. This guarantees the precision and dependability of the ground truth labels linked to each image, which is essential for ensuring the credibility of model training and evaluation. The dataset encompasses a wide spectrum of breast diseases, encompassing both benign and malignant tumors, cysts, fibroadenomas, and other abnormalities. This comprehensive representation accurately mirrors the intricate and diverse nature of real-world clinical settings. By applying preprocessing techniques such as normalization, artifact removal, and data augmentation, the dataset is standardized and improved to reduce differences in imaging settings and maintain uniformity among images. In addition, ethical concerns are thoroughly examined, ensuring that patient privacy and confidentiality are maintained by anonymizing data and adhering to regulatory protocols. The dataset possesses unique attributes such as its size, diversity, annotation quality, and ethical compliance, which make it an invaluable resource for furthering deep learning-based breast cancer diagnosis and enhancing patient care and outcomes.

12.3.2 Deep Learning Architecture

Name the particular architecture of the deep learning model (e.g., CNN, U-Net, or other pertinent models) that is being used for the analysis of breast ultrasonography. The architecture of deep learning (Figure 12.2) consists of many layers, including convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers. In this study, data from breast ultrasound is processed using a deep learning architecture built on convolutional neural networks. CNNs have proven to be quite successful in tasks like feature extraction, segmentation, and image classification. The architecture is specially designed to efficiently detect and classify breast lesions while leveraging XAI methods to guarantee interpretability. It is tailored to match the exact requirements of ultrasound image processing.

12.3.2.1 Convolutional Layers

The several convolutional layers of the CNN structure are responsible for extracting hierarchical information from the input ultrasound images. The convolutional layer uses trainable filters to perform convolution on the input image to extract localized patterns and features at various spatial scales. Activation functions like ReLU are frequently used after convolutional processes to provide non-linearity and enhance the model’s capacity to represent inputs.

12.3.2.2 Pooling Layers

Convolutional layers produce feature maps that are larger than desired. Pooling layers, including max pooling or average pooling, are used to minimize this problem. Pooling approaches reduce the size of feature maps while maintaining the most important properties, which improves computational efficiency and translation invariance.

12.3.2.3 Dense Layers

Often referred to as completely connected layers, dense layers are utilized to group and categorize high-level characteristics that have been gathered from earlier layers. By including dense layers in the model, it becomes possible to identify complex patterns and correlations between features, which in turn permits accurate distinction between different types of breast lesions.

12.3.2.4 Integration of XAI Methods

The architecture not only includes typical CNN layers but also integrates XAI methods to improve interpretability and transparency. XAI tools, such as gradient-based methods like Grad-CAM, attention mechanisms, or model explanation algorithms such as LIME and SHAP, are incorporated into the network to provide visualizations and interpretations of model predictions. The XAI techniques provide insightful information on the particular regions of interest in ultrasound images as well as the attributes that affect the model’s decision-making process. This allows doctors to comprehend and have confidence in the predictions made by the model.

12.3.2.5 Model Optimization and Training

The labeled ultrasound images and the corresponding ground truth annotations are used to train the deep learning architecture. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and Adam are two examples of optimization techniques that are used to gradually appraise the model constraints and diminish the loss function. The generalizability of the model may be improved, and overfitting can be reduced by using regularization techniques like dropout and weight decay.

12.3.2.6 Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)

In SGD, the learning rate (α) multiplied by the gradient of the loss function in relation to each constraint is used to improve the model parameters. The weight update rule for parameter θ at iteration t may be obtained mathematically as follows:

θ (t​+​1) = θ (t) −  α*∇ θ ​L

where ∇ θL denotes the gradient of the loss function L in relation to the parameter θ.

12.3.2.6 Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation)

Adam is an adaptive optimization method that computes unique adaptive learning rates for each parameter by estimating the first and second moments of gradients. The parameter θ update rule in Adam is provided by

n(t​+​1) = β1 * n(t) + (1−β1) * ∇θL
v(t​+​1) = β2 * v(t) + (1−β2) * (∇θL)2
$n = \frac{n\left( {t + 1} \right)}{1 - \beta^{t\! + \! 1}}$
$v = \frac{v\left( {t + 1} \right)}{1 - \beta^{t\! + \! 1}}$
Θ(t​+​1) = Θ(t) − α  *  n/v + €

where n and v are bias-corrected estimates, € is a tiny constant to prevent division by zero, β₁ and β2 are decay rates, and n(t) and v(t) are the first and second instant appraisals of the gradients.

12.3.2.7 Dropout

As a way to avoid overfitting, dropout is a regularization method that arbitrarily eliminates a proportion p of neurons during training. Mathematically, the output of each neuron is multiplied by a binary mask y with probability p:hdropout = γ✶h.

Where γ is drawn from a Bernoulli distribution with probability 1 – p.

12.3.2.8 Weight Decay (L2 Regularization)

By appending a term proportional to the square of the L2 norm of the weights to the loss function, weight decay is a regularization approach that penalizes large weights. The regularized loss function Lreg is given by y:

$L_{reg} = L + \lambda/2\,\sum\limits_{i}^{\theta}\,\,\theta 2i$

where λ is the regularization strength.

12.3.2.8 Assessment and Performance Measures

We test the trained model on a new test set of ultrasound images to see how well it can detect and classify breast cancer. The diagnostic performance and resilience of the model are assessed by computing performance measures such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), and F1 score.

12.3.3 Methods for Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)

The deep learning model has included XAI techniques to improve interpretability. Figure 12.3 represents a summary of the chosen XAI methodologies, including gradient-based methods like Grad-CAM, attention mechanisms, and model explanation techniques such as LIME and SHAP. XAI approaches are used to visualize and comprehend deep learning model predictions, stressing how they have helped to increase dependability and openness. The goal of XAI techniques is to make machine learning models’ decision-making processes transparent so that users can comprehend and rely on the models’ predictions. When XAI approaches are integrated with deep learning-based ultrasound analysis for breast cancer diagnosis, comprehension and interpretation of the data are enhanced. Acquiring acceptability and adoption in therapeutic settings is contingent upon this. Here are several XAI methods that are often used.

12.3.3.1 Gradient-Based Methods

Grad-CAM, or gradient-weighted class activation mapping, is a computer vision technique that emphasizes the regions of an image that are crucial for a neural network’s prediction. Grad-CAM generates class activation maps by computing the gradients of the target class score with respect to the feature maps of the final convolutional layer. This draws attention to the precise regions of the input picture that affect the representation’s computation the most. Grad-CAM generates heatmaps that are difficult to read, while SmoothGrad minimizes the amount of unwanted noise and visual distortions. Consequently, the justifications gain plausibility and consistency.

12.3.3.2 Attention Mechanisms

The self-attention mechanism is a process that assigns different weights of attention to different regions of an input picture. This helps the method to focus on important fragments of the image and ignore irrelevant information. Another type of model that can use spatial transformations to dynamically alter input images is called a spatial transformer. By intelligently aligning and cropping regions of interest, this model enables improved feature extraction and classification.

12.3.3.3 Techniques for Explaining Models

A technique called limited interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) provides human-understandable descriptions for particular model estimates. This is accomplished by first producing altered samples around the particular instance of interest and then simulating the behavior of the complex model in that restricted region using a basic interpretable model. Shapley standards, which are derived from cooperative game theory, are used by the computational technique Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) to quantify the effect of every attribute on a model’s output. SHAP standards deliver a thorough understanding of the importance of the features and the influence of their interactions within the model.

12.3.3.4 Rule-Based Approaches

Decision rules are derived from the decision limits of a trained model. They offer clear and easily understandable criteria for making decisions in classification tasks, making them transparent and accessible to humans. Symbolic rule extraction methods produce symbolic rules or decision trees from opaque models, providing a clear description of the model’s decision-making process.

12.3.3.5 Visualizations and Explanations

Activation maps depict the activation patterns of individual neurons or channels in the deep learning model, offering insights into the properties identified at various layers of the network. Feature relevance plots rank and visually represent the relevance of input characteristics by measuring their impact on model predictions. They are useful for selecting features and gaining insights into model behavior.

12.3.3.6 Model Training and Evaluation

They provide a detailed explanation of the training process, taking into account the batch size, learning rate, number of epochs, and optimization method. Examine a number of regularization strategies, including weight decay and dropout, which are meant to reduce overfitting. Enumerate the evaluation metrics (specificity, sensitivity, accuracy, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) that are applied to evaluate the performance of the deep learning model (AUC-ROC). The validation set, often referred to in the context of cross-validation, is used to determine the generalizability of the model and modify its hyperparameters.

12.3.3.7 Training Procedure

For breast ultrasound analysis, the deep learning model is trained using labeled ultrasound images and the accompanying ground truth annotations. The dataset is usually divided into three groups: test, validation, and training sets. Typically, the training set contains between 70% and 80% of the data. Optimization techniques such as Adam, RMSprop, and SGD are used to reduce the loss function and iteratively inform the classical parameters. The validation set is used to optimize the model’s performance by adjusting hyperparameters such batch size, epoch count, and learning rate.

12.3.3.8 Data augmentation and Regularization

Rotation, scaling, flipping, translation, and other techniques are applied to add greater variety and resilience to the training dataset. Regularization methods, including weight decay, batch normalization, and dropout, are employed to reduce overfitting and enhance a model’s capacity for generalization. To prevent the coadaptation of features, dropout is utilized to arbitrarily deactivate a subset of neurons during training. Batch normalization helps in smoothing and quickening the training process by regularizing each layer’s activations. Large weights are penalized by weight decay, commonly referred to as L2 regularization, which reduces overfitting and increases sparsity.

12.3.3.9 Validation and Hyperparameter Tuning

The purpose of the validation set is to determine the optimal hyperparameters and assess the model’s performance throughout training. By evaluating the outcomes on the validation set, hyperparameters like the learning rate, dropout rate, and network design are changed to increase the model’s ability to generalize. Some tactics that may be used to reduce overfitting and improve convergence include learning rate scheduling and early stopping.

12.3.3.10 Model Evaluation

A unique test set of ultrasound pictures that were not seen during the training or validation phase is used to evaluate the learned model. The diagnostic performance of the model is evaluated by the computation of performance indicators, which include specificity, sensitivity, accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), and F1 score. ROC curves and confusion matrices are frequently used to visually depict a model’s classification performance at different thresholds. Techniques like paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests can be used to measure the performance of many models or experimental conditions using statistical significance testing. XAI techniques are included in the evaluation pipeline to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model’s decision-making process. Transparency and dependability are increased by producing visualizations and interpretations of the model’s calculations through the use of gradient-based algorithms, attention processes, and model explanation tools. One can conduct a qualitative study of explanations given by XAI to verify the model’s reasoning and detect possible flaws or biases.

12.3.4 Experimental Configuration

The experimental setting required meticulous planning and configuration to guarantee accurate outcomes in the deep learning-based ultrasound analysis for breast cancer screening. The hardware utilized comprised NVIDIA GPUs equipped with CUDA support, enabling efficient model training and evaluation.

To conduct the study, current training on breast cancer prediction was followed. There are several deep learning and machine learning techniques available for cancer detection and prediction. Preprocessing techniques like the label encoder and normalizer method were applied to handle the data efficiently. The bar graph in Figure 12.4 displays the total number of benign and malignant cells in the dataset that was obtained.

Several machine learning approaches were used to predict breast cancer on the Wisconsin dataset, including K-nearest neighbor, support vector machine (SVM), decision tree, Naïve Bayes, logistic regression, and random forest. The greatest accuracy achieved by the random forest and SVM algorithms was 96.5%. Using deep learning techniques, the forecast accuracy was increased. In Figures 12.5 and 12.6, the accuracy and loss of the model are graphically represented in proportion to the number of epochs. As the number of epochs increases, the model’s accuracy rises and its loss falls.

The CNN model yielded an accuracy of 97.3%, while the ANN model produced an accuracy of 99.3%, indicating greater efficiency compared to the machine learning methods mentioned earlier. ReLU and sigmoid are examples of activation functions that were used in deep learning, demonstrating greater efficiency. Consider the given input image (Figure 12.7) as it is passed into the developed model for predicting the presence of breast cancer.

12.3.4.1 Probability of Predicted Output

Figure 12.8 shows the probability comparison of different classes. The maximum accuracy achieved was 96.5%.

12.4 Conclusion

Beyond its interpretability and diagnostic accuracy, the combination of deep learning-based ultrasound analysis with XAI approaches offers substantial advantages for clinical practice. By providing concise justifications for diagnostic results, XAI enhances clinician confidence in AI-assisted diagnostics and facilitates seamless incorporation into conventional healthcare procedures. Furthermore, real-world input facilitates the iterative creation and adaptation of these models to evolving clinical demands and challenges. This means that, in addition to improving the efficacy and precision of breast cancer diagnosis, this technology may also encourage innovation in the delivery of oncology therapy, ultimately benefiting patients.

13 Explainable Artificial Intelligence Techniques in Deep Learning-Based Liver Tumor Analysis

R. Manjula Devi
S. Dheenathayalan

Abstract

As medical imaging technology develops, artificial intelligence (AI) can help radiologists and physicians classify liver tumors accurately and significantly. However, the inherent intricacy of AI models, primarily deep learning algorithms, commonly precludes their adoption because their decision-making processes are opaque and difficult to explain. This chapter proposes a complete architecture that achieves high classification accuracy and offers interpretable perceptions of the model’s choice, addressing the important requirement for explainable AI in liver tumor classification. The proposed system combines existing deep learning architectures with cutting-edge explainable AI (XAI) XAI methods to produce a hybrid model that syndicates predicted accuracy with understandable validations. The model may concentrate on essential areas of medical images and emphasize discriminative features that contribute to its classification conclusions because the framework implements attention mechanisms and feature visualization techniques.

Keywords: Model clarification, convolutional neural networks, SHapley Additive exPlanations, local interpretable model-agnostic explanations, partial dependence plots,

13.1 Introduction

The use of machine learning (ML) algorithms has increased over the past decades because artificial intelligence (AI) has seen tremendous and ongoing advancement. These astounding achievements are closely related to opaque, black-box AI models and increased model complexity proposed by Bakrania et al. [1]. It is necessary to develop solutions that can help overcome such a challenge to boost the usage of AI systems in delicate and significant fields like healthcare and security, where extra requirements must be met in addition to high accuracy. AI that can explain its decisions or forecasts to human users is known as explainable AI (XAI). XAI aims to improve the openness, dependability, and accountability of AI systems, mainly when applied in high-risk fields like security, finance, or healthcare. The process used in explainable AI is depicted in Figure 13.1. Various methods inspect the liver tumor before the medical data is provided to the XAI framework proposed by Peng et al. [2]. The clinicians are then given the proposed XAI technique’s computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) results. Finally, medical professionals use CAD to support the diagnosis and treatment of the liver.

The exercise data will be provided as an input in XAI-based techniques. Based on the requirements, the internal workings of the model are developed to describe the workings of the output interface. As a result, XAI’s users are aware of its effects, boosting trust in AI systems. Users can increase the accuracy of the results and reveal model defects based on the understanding of the output, which will help users make the best decision for model improvement. The proposed XAI model is outlined in Figure 13.2. To recover the medical understanding of the liver tumor, the proposed paradigm dispenses both global and local explanations.

Data collection and preprocessing are done to acquire the patient records. The model is then loaded to forecast how the exacerbation risk will pan out. The global and local explanations are then obtained using the model explanation technique. The results of the model and the explanation will then be reviewed and further validated by the radiologist.

13.2 Literature Review

Ahmed and Shelly [3] created a stack-ensemble-based ML model framework using XAI to depict the association between the risk factors for lung cancer and the spatial distribution of LBC. The XAI in the disciplines of drugs, psychology, medical structures, and other areas is explained by [4]. However, prognostics and health management (PHM) did not offer the analytical method to decrease patient waiting times, enhance services, boost productivity in telemedicine, and increase accuracy, speed, and efficiency.

Andreu-Perez and Emberson [5] created an XAI-based model for investigating the development and functionality of baby brain images captured by near-infrared spectroscopy. Atul Anand and Tushar Kadian [6] proposed deep neural networks for identifying heart diseases using ECG signals. Bakrania et al. [1] discussed the challenges of AI in liver cancer diagnosis and management. In addition, they discussed the future perspectives of AI application in liver cancer and how a multidisciplinary approach using AI in nanomedicine could accelerate the transition of personalized liver cancer medicine from bench side to the clinic. Kumar et al. [7] proposed investigating the applicability of AI techniques in photovoltaic systems. Fang and Tan [8] created a model to employ patient characteristics to determine the likelihood that a specific disease would progress. However, they need more transparency in clinical practice.

Introduced a classifier based on the convolutional neural network for finding lashes and outlined the saliency maps used to trace the output of the model. Jahmunah et al. [9]have created dense net and CNN models to predict abnormalities in EEG signals. In healthcare applications, AI and ML are crucial, and hence, XAI is employed to earn the conviction of AI models. It will increase confidence in extrapolative models in real-world scenarios.

Conducted research on skin malignancies for both males and females. In their work, biomarkers were used for predicting skin cancer, along with trained XGboost ML models. Jahmunah and Ng [11] discussed the ideas and methods of XAI-based cardiology. Kute and Pradhan [12] proposed that XAI is characterized by knowledge- and data-based strategies. Knowledge-driven XAI requires knowledge about how to explain, whereas data-driven XAI needs local, global, and instance-specific procedures for explanation. They used the publicly accessible PTB-XL output dataset. XAI explanation was given a new meaning by Merry and Riddle [13]. Miro-Nicolau and Moya-Alcover [14] observed the results using XAI chest images. X-ray images were represented using class activation maps (CAM) in their work. Obayya and Nemri [15] developed XAI approaches in teleophthalmology. The accuracy of the categorization model was 98.24% by utilizing the SPECT MPI pictures. Papandrianos Feleki [16] created a deep XAI approach to envisage coronary artery disease (CAD).

Peng and Zou [2] proposed a framework combining global and local interpretable methods to improve the transparency of complex models and gain insight into the judgments from these models, thereby guiding treatment strategies and improving the prognosis of hepatitis patients. Pertzborn and Arolt [17] presented a VGG 19 model to detect malignancies. In their work, deep learning-based models combined with XAI techniques and preprocessing data led to an accuracy of 80%. According to Lombardi and Diacono [18], it is possible to predict Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and cognitive impairment using XAI. The disease has been identified using random forest classifiers. Datasets for monitoring patients' health are gathered from various sources. Some information is collected through sensors, while other data comes directly from clinical trials and other studies proposed by Yang [19]. To identify and perceive brain cancers in clinical areas, Zeineldin et al. [20] developed an XAI framework in neurology for analyzing brain tumors.

13.3 Proposed Methodology

The progress of a CAD system for CT liver diagnosis based on AI has advanced significantly in recent years. Due to the nonlinearity of the clinical data collected from hospitals, deep learning-based models perform better than ML methods. However, radiologists are suspicious of complicated models because they operate like a black box that superintends the reasons behind their decisions. Hence, this chapter proposes an XAI framework to address these problems by providing global and local interpretations of liver tumor diagnoses while maintaining high prediction accuracy. First, the framework’s viability is examined using a public dataset collected from a multispecialty scan center. Both apparent and black-box ML models are used to better the classification performance. Finally, the SHapley Additive exPlanations and partial dependence plots are utilized to enhance the model interpretation of liver tumors. In the proposed system, the data taken from the patient is initially stored in the design and given to the XAI framework for further processing, and the results are again stored in the server. Then, it is fed as an input to the CAD system. Once the results are obtained from the CAD system, the radiologist compares the results obtained from the XAI framework and CAD system. The suggested prototype offers global and local explanations to enhance medical empathy of the risk prediction for liver tumors. Data collection and preparation are used to create patient records. The model is then loaded to forecast how the exacerbation risk will pan out. The global and local explanations are then obtained using the model explanation technique. Doctors receive them to examine and further validate the prediction and explanation outcomes.

13.3.1 Dataset Description

In this work, CT abdomen images are obtained from the freely available database (https://www.ircad.fr/research/data-sets/liver-segmentation-3d-ircadb-01/) 3DIRCADB (3D image reconstruction for comparison of algorithm database) and the private dataset obtained from multispecialty scan centres. Compared with the other challenge datasets, the 3DIRCADB dataset has a higher diversity and complexity of livers and lesions. The widely available 3DIRCADB dataset encloses 20 venous phases enhanced CT scans of the liver hepatic tumors of 75% of cases by considering 10 women and 10 men. The dimension of the slice is 511 × 511 pixels, with height and width varying from 0.55 to 0.89 mm and the width between adjacent slices ranging from 1.4 to 5.1 mm. Since the 3DIRCADB dataset offered improved diversity and difficulty of livers and their tumors, it is considered a challenging database. Besides, the dataset collected from the scan center encompasses 130 scans of different patients. A minimum of 84 slices per patient are regarded with the expert segmentations manually provided by the radiologist. These images are obtained from Arthi Scan Center Chennai, Tamilnadu, India.

13.3.2 Preprocessing

Preprocessing is a significant phase to enhance image quality and increase image analysis performance. Recently, several denoising techniques have been proposed for removing Gaussian noise. Moreover, numerous 2D wavelet-based denoising methods have also been established to alter the image into multiple subbands at different angles. Then, each subband’s wavelet coefficients are applied to a denoising procedure. These filters effectively smooth the noise but still have difficulty blurring the edges within the images. This work employs a block-based non-local means (NLM) algorithm , median filtering with pixel modelling technique as shown in Figure 13.3.

13.3.2.1 Block-Based Non-local Means Algorithm

The traditional NLM algorithm may lead to poor results because of its nonlocality of neighboring pixels. To overcome this, a block-based NLM method is proposed, significantly reducing the computational time. The block-based NLM filter is more concrete in MRI and CT images since they are primarily 3D or stacks of 2D. Thus, in biomedical image denoising, computational efficiency is vital. To maintain global continuity, this work overlaps adjacent blocks by one column or row of pixels. The multiple approximations of the restored intensity value at the pixel xi are then averaged among several approximations. While dealing with large datasets, averaging intensity values produces high computational costs.

Therefore, rather than considering pixels, an enhanced NLM is suggested using blocks of size (2α + 1)2 with overlapping constraints. Later, the NLM restoration is performed on these blocks rather than on pixels. The block-based enhanced NLM method is described by

(13.1)$NL\left\lbrack u \right\rbrack\left( B_{ik} \right) = \sum\limits_{B_{j}\epsilon\ v_{ik}}^{}w\left( {B_{ik},\, B_{j}} \right)\ u\left( B_{j} \right)$

where

$w\left( {B_{ik,}\ B_{j,}} \right) = \left\{ {\frac{1}{Z_{ik}}e^{- \frac{\parallel {u{(B_{ik})} - u{(B_{j})} \parallel^{2}}}{\widehat{h}}}\ \ 0} \right.\,\,{otherwise\; if}\;\mu_{1} < \frac{u\left( \underset{\_}{B_{ik}} \right)}{u\left( B_{j} \right)} < \frac{1}{\mu_{1}}\;{and}\;\sigma_{1}^{2} < \frac{\operatorname{var}\left( {u\left( B_{ik} \right)} \right)}{\operatorname{var}\left( {u\left( B_{j} \right)} \right)} < \frac{1}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}$

Zik is a constant of normalization satisfying ∑Bjϵ vikw(Bik, Bj) = 1 and ĥ is a parameter for smoothness. In addition, the most similar neighborhoods are selected well in advance to avoid unnecessary weight computation. The weight factors are computed only when the ratio of the mean and variance of u(Bik) and u(Bj) are in the range of 1.

13.3.2.2 Thresholding Using Median Filtering with Pixel Modeling (MF–PM) Technique in the Wavelet Domain

Initially, the wavelet transform is applied to the CT abdomen image. Then, the high-frequency subbands are denoised using adaptive thresholding with the Bayes shrinkage function. Finding the optimal threshold value is essential for preserving clinical details and noise suppression. This work obtains the threshold value using noise variance and the standard deviation of noise-free images. Let us consider that α is the threshold value, and it is given by

(13.2)$\alpha = \frac{\sigma_{\vartheta}^{2}}{\sigma_{y}}$

where, α is the noise variance that is estimated by the robust median estimation method and it is given by

(13.3)${\,\sigma\,}_{\vartheta}^{2} = \left( \frac{{median(}\left| {x\left( {m,n} \right)} \right|}{0.6475} \right)^{\! 2}$

x(m,n) ̴ HL represents the level in the wavelet domain. The standard deviation of the noise-free image is given by

(13.4)σ y2 = max(σ x2 − σ ϑ2, 0 )

where

$\sigma_{x}^{2} = \frac{1}{N}\sum\limits_{i\! = \! 1}^{N}X_{i}^{2}$ and N represents an input image. Then the thresholding function is given by

(13.5)X̂ = {0 f|X| ≤ α signum(x)(|X| − αf|X| > α

The obtained results show that the preprocessing results of the proposed median filtering with pixel modeling (MF-PM) technique yield better performance when compared to other methods. The edge details are preserved in this method by considering the pixel array-based filtering technique. However, in the NLM technique, the factual edges vanish due to the significant value of the standard deviation of the Gaussian filter.

13.3.3 Deep Learning Model-Based Image Prediction

In this work, the cascaded encoder-decoder CNN (CEDCNN) method is engaged for effective liver segmentation and tumors from CT abdomen images. The CEDCNN structure is composed of an encoder and decoder network, which are symmetric, as shown in Figure 13.4. The proposed architecture resembles the SegNet model. In the conventional SegNet architecture, the first 14 convolutional layers are used by the encoder-network component of a traditional SegNet design. Because the encoder and decoder networks are symmetrical, the decoder network includes 13 convolutional layers. The softmax classifier function uses the decoder network output to generate a probability class for all pixels. Then, a convolution-based filter bank extracts the normalized feature map. In this work, the rectified linear nonlinearity (ReLU) unit is followed by batch normalization. Finally, the ReLU is subjected to max pooling with window size 2 × 2 and stride 2, followed by subsampling. The decoder network upsamples the input feature maps. A decoder filter bank creates the dense feature map by applying a convolution operator to the upsampling. Each of these feature maps is also subjected to batch normalization. The final stage of the decoder network yields a multichannel feature map that resembles an input image. The softmax classifier function uses this multichannel feature map to identify the pixels in the input image.

Figure 13.5 illustrates the model used by the CEDCNN approach, which consists of 41 layers: 3 FC (fully connected) layers, 2 × 2 maxpooling, and 13 convolutional layers. SegNet, an encoder-decoder technique suggested by VGG-16, uses predefined weights. It has a classification layer based on pixels as well as an encoder-decoder network. Convolution and max pooling will occur at the encoder network since VGG-16 is the encoder portion, which has 13 convolutional layers. Additionally, a 2 × 2 max pooling is carried out, leading to the corresponding storage of indices. The decoder network maps using a resolution encoder and then provides the results to the classification layers.

13.3.3.1 Training

A random selection of 15 sets comprising 2,234 cuts was utilized for training, while the remaining five sets with 591 slices were used for testing in this study. Additionally, during the CEDCNN training, no data augmentation is utilized. During the training phase, the two-fold normalization approach is used for the CT image (I) and the related ground truth image (G). Finally, each CT image and ground truth image is divided into different slices with an image size of 256 × 256 before starting the training phase. The input is provided with the normalized 2D images and ground truth sets to fit a rough segmentation model. This model primarily distinguishes between liver and background characteristics.

On the other hand, any 3D volume must meet specific requirements. Each 3D volume must be resized to a voxel size of 1 mm3. Finally, the normalized images are cropped using the liver mask. A dense training approach is adopted to fit an acceptable liver segmentation model. The stochastic gradient descent method is used as an optimizer during training. The learning rate progressively reduces every 50 epochs from 0.1 to 0.00450, with a 0.4 drop factor. The network is trained for 150 epochs with a batch size of 8. The first CNN output is a binary representation of expected liver areas, which are then utilized as input to the CNN by extracting ROIs.

13.3.3.2 Testing

The liver region will be segmented from abdominal images during the testing stage. As in the training stage, in the testing phase, two-fold image normalization is also done once the 3D testing images are normalized into 2D slices. Then, a coarse liver segmentation is predicted using the trained structure. Alternatively, the input CT and roughly segmented liver images are resized to a regularized voxel size. Finally, the trained 3D fully convolutional neural network produces fine and rough liver tumor segmentation.

13.3.3.3 Performance Evaluation Metrics

The performance of the proposed preprocessing, liver segmentation, and tumor segmentation methods is analyzed based on the following measures.

13.3.3.4 Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR)

The peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is a performance indicator that measures how the mean square errors introduced into the original image throughout the filtering process compare to the square of the maximum pixel value. The PSNR is given as follows:

(13.6)${PSNR}\left( {dB} \right) = 10\,{lo}g_{10}\frac{{ma}x^{2}}{MSE}$

where "max" indicates the maximum pixel value of the input image, and PSNR suggests the quality of the reconstructed image. The increased PSNR value results in the enhanced quality of the image.

13.3.3.5 Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASD)

It calculates the surface distance based on the voxels of two segmentations by considering the average of all saved distances. The average value of all stored distances is zero, and this indicates perfect segmentation.

It is one of the most commonly used measures in terms of mm, as follows:

(13.7)$\frac{{ASD}\left( {mm} \right) = {{\sum_{x\epsilon X}{min}}_{y\epsilon Y}\left( {d\left( {x,y} \right)} \right) + \sum_{y\epsilon Y}{min}_{x\epsilon X}\left( {d\left( {x,y} \right)} \right)}}{N_{X} + N_{Y}}$

where X and Y indicate the reference surface and segmented volume surface, x and y represent the mesh points of X and Y, d(x, y) indicates the distance between x and y, then NX and NY are the number of points on X and Y, respectively.

13.3.3.6 Root Mean-Squared Symmetric Surface Distance (RMSD)

It measures the surface difference between two different segmentations by considering the surface distance. It is required to square the surface voxels before storing them. It is premeditated as an equation in terms of mm:

(13.8) ${RMSD}\left( {mm} \right) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{x\epsilon X}^{}\min_{y\epsilon Y}\left( {d\left( {x,y} \right)} \right)^{2} + \sum_{y\epsilon Y}^{}\min_{x\epsilon X}\left( {d\left( {x,y} \right)} \right)^{2}}{N_{X} + N_{Y}}}$

13.3.3.7 Maximum Symmetric Surface Distance (MSD)

It is a measure based on the Euclidean distance. It is defined as the difference between the surface voxels. Then, the maximum surface value provides the maximum MSD. It is calculated as in eq. (13.9):

(13.9)MSD(mm) = max (maxxϵX(minyϵY(d(x,y))),maxyϵY(d(x,y)))

13.3.3.8 Volumetric Overlap Error (VOE)

This metric measures the difference in volume between the reference image and the volume of the liver-segmented image. To measure this metric, the average of all slices is considered for measuring the metrics in terms of percentage of error. It is calculated as follows:

(13.10)${VOE}(\%) = \left( {1 - \frac{V_{seg} \cap V_{ref}}{V_{seg} \cup V_{ref}}} \right) \times 100$

where Vseg is the segmented image and Vref is the reference image. This method effectively shows the segmentation accuracy. If the volumetric overlap error is zero, it indicates segmentation accuracy.

13.3.3.9 Signed Relative Volume Difference (SRVD)

It measures the volume difference between the segmented and input images. It is expressed in terms of percentage and is calculated as in eq. (13.11):

(13.11)${SRVD}\left( \% \right) = \frac{\left| {v_{seg} - v_{ref}} \right|}{v_{ref}} \times 100$

Based on these measures, the performance of the proposed techniques is evaluated. A smaller value in all evaluation metrics leads to a better segmentation result.

13.3.4 Tumor Classification Module

The main intention of the classification module is to differentiate the type of tumor present in the segmented tumor image. Classification of the tumor is the final stage in the CAD model. The difference in features extracted from the segmented liver tumor is given as input to the classifier stage in this stage. The essential task in the tumor classification stage is the extraction and selection of features. In this work, multilayer perceptron (MLP), support vector machine (SVM), and kappa statistics, random forest (RF) techniques are employed for classifying liver tumors.

In the existing work, the classification is done only by extracting the features from the lesion ROI. However, the novelty in this classification stage is considering two ROIs, which improves the accuracy by taking the difference of features extracted from the lesion and liver region. Initially, there are two types of ROI: one is a lesion (R1), and the other is surrounding normal liver tissue (R2). The features obtained using the first and second ROI will work as a novel feature vector. However, for identifying the normal liver tissue (R2), it is necessary to follow some constraints:

  • The ratio between the lesion ROI (R1) and the specific liver region (R2) is to be chosen as 1:1.7 by conducting several trials.

  • The typical liver region (R2) must centrally surround the lesion ROI (R1).

  • The lesion region (R1) is expelled from the typical liver region (R2).

In this manner, the features extracted from each of the tumor region and the surrounding region are considered to be a new feature vector.

13.4 Explainability Model

Model-agnostic interpretation techniques, which have recently been made possible by breakthroughs in ML, are used to explain complex models while maintaining good prediction performance. Separating the explanation model from the model-agnostic interpretation is more flexible than the model-specific explanation method. The two types of model-agnostic interpretation techniques are local explanation and global explanation. The most popular local explanation technique is local interpretable model-agnostic explanations(LIME). The two most common global interpretable techniques are PDP (partial dependence plots) and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations).

13.4.1 LIME Model

To provide interpretability for complicated models, LIME trains local surrogate models. LIME first produces a fresh dataset through data disruption. LIME then uses the new dataset to train an interpretable model, such as a decision tree. Finally, the black box model’s equivalent prediction performance is contrasted with the objective of the interpretable model. LIME is defined as follows:

(13.12)γ(x) = argmin L( f​, g, Πx) + Ω(g)gϵG

where L is the loss function. The explainable model for instance x is represented by g. The interpretable model family is denoted as G. The closeness of the experimented instances to instance x is indicated by the instances x. Ω (g) defines the intricacy of model g.

13.4.2 PDP Model

PDP illustrates the small impact of a feature on the outcome predicted by a sophisticated ML model. It shows how the input and output are related to one another, whether it is more complicated, monotonous, or linear. The partial dependence function $\widetilde{f_{x_{s}}}$ is given by the definition of

(13.13) $\widetilde{f_{x_{s}}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i\! = \! 1}^{n}\ \widetilde{f_{x_{s}}}\left( {x_{s,}x_{c}^{i}} \right)$

where $\widetilde{f_{x_{s}}}$ is the process that generates the overall relationship between an input feature and the expected result. The feature set “S” encompassing one or two features, xs denotes the set of features to be plotted $\widetilde{f_{x_{s}}}$. xc designates the remaining features in the model, and n is the number of instances used in the dataset.

13.4.3 SHAP Model

It measures the impact of the feature on the multifaceted model with SHapley values. The sum of marginal aids is referred to as a SHapley value. It can be identified by the measure of closeness of prediction across all potential coalitions. The SHapley value is calculated by

(13.14)$\varnothing_{j}\left( x \right) = \sum\limits_{s\complement{\{{x1,x2.\ .\ .,xm}\}}{\{ x_{j}\}}}^{}\frac{\left| s \right|!\left( {m - \left| s \right| - 1} \right)!}{m!}\left( {{val}\left( {s \cup \left\{ x_{j} \right\} - {value}\left( s \right)} \right)} \right)$

where S is the SHapley value of xj, xj signifies a feature value, a feature subset of the model is represented by “s,” the number of features is denoted by m, and the value is the predicted feature values in set s.

13.4.4 Results of Predicted Model

In this work, the interpretable framework is practiced in a Python environment. Using K-fold cross-validation, the overall accuracy of the complex models was determined. K is typically set to 5, 10, or 20. Table 13.5 evaluates the interpretable models using the liver dataset.

13.5 Conclusion

In this work, an explainable ML framework combines CEDCNN-based models with recently discovered explanation techniques to accurately predict the probability of liver diseases. The suggested framework is tested using public datasets from standard databases and nonpublic datasets collected from multidisciplinary scan centers. According to the results, the RF classifier method achieves the highest overall accuracy of 99.5% using a deep learning framework and an average accuracy of 95.4% using the XAI model with an RF-based classifier. The results of the proposed framework clarifications are reliable with the characteristics of liver tumors, which may help the radiologist to make more accurate diagnoses. In addition, this method promotes the application of AI in healthcare by highlighting the benefits of XAI frameworks in deciphering black-box models like RF. This work can be extended in the future by collecting more real-time liver images and investigating cutting-edge, model-independent techniques.
