14 A Novel African Wild Dog Optimization (AWDO) Algorithm for Applications of Artificial Intelligence

Prabakaran
Senthil Kumaran
Shyamala

Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) harbors the potential to tackle intricate challenges and enhance human capabilities across various domains. Through its significant capabilities, AI plays a crucial role in data analysis, natural language processing (NLP), healthcare, and other decision-based fields. The primary objective of AI in these domains is to render precise decisions promptly. The attainment of higher decision-making accuracy and system performance enhancement necessitates the utilization of optimization algorithms to aid in the decision-making process efficiently. Swarm optimization draws inspiration from the collective behavior of animals or insects that cooperate in hunting, thereby facilitating rapid decision-making. This chapter delves into diverse swarm optimization algorithms that support decision-making processes in AI applications and introduces a novel algorithm called African wild dog optimization (AWDO). The proposed AWDO algorithm is an energy-efficient swarm optimization technique that minimizes energy consumption by AI nodes or neurons, resulting in expedited search outcomes. The efficacy of the AWDO algorithm is evaluated against established optimization algorithms like particle swarm optimization, ant colony optimization (ACO), artificial bee colony (ABC) optimization algorithm, firefly algorithm, and bacterial foraging optimization (BFO) algorithms in the realm of healthcare diagnosis applications.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence, African wild dog optimization, particle swarm optimization, ant colony optimization, artificial bee colony, firefly algorithm, bacterial foraging optimization, healthcare diagnosis,

14.1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) [1] is an inevitably developing technology that creates the possibility for machines to learn from occurrences and make decisions on real-time events. The proliferation of AI has made it possible to make vital decisions and diagnoses in business and intelligence systems. Some of the vital applications of AI are market prediction, supply chain management, medical diagnosis, traffic analysis, image-based diagnosis, etc. Among the various applications, AI holds a major role in healthcare diagnosis systems, which involve cancer detection, early tumor detection, and many more related applications. Varieties of AI algorithms such as Naïve Bayes, support vector machine (SVM) [2], random forest (RF) [3], decision tree (DT) [4], neural networks (NN) [5], and deep learning (DL) algorithms [6] like convolutional neural networks (CNN) and recurrent neural networks (RNN) have been employed for the aforementioned applications.

Machine learning (ML) and the DL algorithm, which are subsets of the AI)technique, were applied for the diagnosis of multiple diseases from medical multimodal images. These multiple diseases include cancer, tumors, and other diseases at earlier stages. The medical image diagnosis is performed based on the dimension, region of interest (RoI), and the histogram [7] of the image pixel. The major challenge associated with AI-based medical image diagnosis is the feature selection process, as it often misses major and essential features for the classification process. Diseases like tumors necessitate the structural features of the tumor. The general structure of performing medical image diagnosis using an AI algorithm is depicted in Figure 14.1.

The computer-assisted diagnosis of human disease exhibits various advantages in terms of knowledge as well as accuracy in the classification process. However, the classification process is a complex one as it relies on various parameters. The most important aspect of the learning algorithms is the training of the model. The existing models were trained using the free datasets that were relevant to the particular type of human disease. Based on the volume of training data, the rate of accuracy of the diagnosis system [8] varies. In addition to the training data, the efficiency of the diagnosis model relies on the type of algorithm used for classification purposes. The algorithms of the DL model do not require any explicit input features, as they employ the features of the deep neural networks (DNN). The DNN employs multiple layers, namely “n” number of layers, for extracting the features from the input medical image. From the extracted features, the DNN model performs the feature selection process for efficient classification and diagnosis. Despite the advantages of DL in the medical image diagnosis process, it experiences major challenges of shortfall in terms of accuracy due to the feature selection process and the degradation of edges of the input images. This causes essential images to deteriorate in terms of efficiency and thus necessitates the requirement of advanced AI technology [9] for efficient and accurate medical image diagnosis. The existing methodologies fall short in terms of global search, impacting the accuracy in the diagnosis process. In addition, the optimization function [10] is trapped under the local optima, thus leading to weak characteristics in robustness to the local optima. The major objectives of the proposed work are to classify the medical images with an enhanced level of accuracy using the African wild dog optimization (AWDO) algorithm. The proposed method is highly robust in preserving the features of the input image. In addition to the increase in accuracy, the proposed work excels in terms of precision, recall, and biopsy rate. The organization of this chapter is structured with a basic introduction in Section 14.1, literature analysis in Section 14.2, and a detailed description of the proposed novel AWDO algorithm in Section 14.3. The case study is performed, and the analysis of the proposed work is presented in Section 14.4. The chapter is concluded with the highlights of the proposed work in Section 14.5.

14.2 Literature Review

The smart medication process followed over the past decade motivates numerous researchers to employ and introduce novel classification algorithms in diagnosing specific diseases in human beings. This section illustrates the notable research results of AI in terms of medical image diagnosis, such as tumor detection and cancer detection.

Jabbar et al. [11] proposed a Caps-VGGNet hybrid model [11] for the diagnosis of tumor detection. The authors employed the Brats dataset for training the model, and the major challenge of the introduced model is the requirement of a huge volume of data for training the model to achieve a high level of accuracy. Mo et al. [12] proposed a Hover-Trans block extraction model [12] to determine breast cancer at an earlier stage. The authors employed the GDPH dataset for training the model and used sonogram images for the detection process. Li et al. [13] developed a frequency-guided diffusion model [13] for processing and diagnosing medical images. The proposed model is capable of diagnosing any type of medical disease, provided the system is fed with the appropriate training datasets. Wu et al. [14] introduced a nonlocal algorithm [14] based on AI techniques to detect anomalies in human MRI images. The proposed model is highly robust and optimized the boundaries of the input image.

Asiri et al. [15] introduced a dual computerized model [15] for enhancing the accuracy of the diagnosis of input medical images. The first model aims at the image enhancement process using neural networks and the principal component analysis method. The latter model employs the support vector machine for performing the classification of the input tumor image. The classification is performed after the segmentation process and achieved an accuracy of 89.9%. Shamsad et al. (2024) contributed to early medical image diagnosis by designing an AI-based transfer learning model [16]. The proposed model aimed to enhance the accuracy in detecting anomalies in input medical images. The authors employed VGG-16 and VGG-19 datasets for training and testing the proposed model.

Palkar et al. [17] designed a Glioma prognosis model [17] using the AI technique. The proposed work was compared with existing AI models like random forest, support vector machine, CatBoost, LGBM classifier, and XGBoost to prove its supremacy in terms of accuracy in classifying the input medical image. Asif et al. [18] employed AI tools [18] for analyzing biomedical datasets in diagnosing medical images at the early stages. The authors employed ML and DL models for the diagnosis of HCC images.

Prakash et al. [19] presented an advanced framework for the medical image diagnosis process using the generative adversarial network (GAN) model [19]. The proposed GAN model is a three-dimensional model that accepts CT images of the kidney to detect and predict the presence of tumors in the kidney. The authors employed a structural GAN model to produce a minimum of 20% enhancement in the accuracy of the prediction process. Siddique et al. [20] introduced an innovative training model using the Inception V3 model [20] and employed the particle swarm optimization algorithm for detecting and classifying anomalies in tumors in various parts of the human body. The authors employed the INCEPT training model and achieved an accuracy of 90.5%.

The major drawbacks of the existing AI-based medical image diagnosis model are as follows.

  • The existing classification model employs excessive classification parameters, leading to an increase in the complexity of the model.

  • The rate of convergence of the existing models is very slow, and the optimization rate is considerably low.

  • The robustness of the existing works was low, and it feels hard to diagnose the noisy input medical images.

  • Due to the decrease in the level of robustness, the level of accuracy also sheds to a greater extent.

To overcome the above-mentioned challenges of the existing classification methods, the AWDO is employed to achieve the following contributions in the medical image diagnosis process.

  • The proposed AWDO classification algorithm is highly robust and will accept noisy input medical images for the classification process.

  • The proposed AWDO algorithm accepts minimal parameters, which possess the least complexity in terms of the classification process.

  • The proposed AWDO is a promising optimization technique with the potential to provide efficient and effective solutions to a wide range of challenging problems.

14.3 Proposed Model

The proposed AWDO is a metaheuristic algorithm designed based on the inspiration of the hunting behavior of African dogs. This intelligent algorithm demonstrates the team work efforts of the African dogs, its adaptability, and its efficiency in hunting its prey. A similar pattern is employed in the proposed work to determine the anomalous behavior of the input medical image. In this proposed scheme of the optimization process, the swarm of African dogs, namely 5–20 dogs, is directed by the pair of leader dogs as depicted in Figure 14.2. The leader dogs organize the member dogs and act as the best pairs of dogs in the hunting process. The leader dog pairs perform decision-making processes, controlling the member dogs, and hunting and resting processes. Inspired by this hunting behavior, the proposed AWDO algorithm identifies the anomalous behavior or pattern of the input medical image by employing a pair of threshold pixels, namely threshold pixel-row wise (PR) and threshold pixel-column wise (PC). Based on the threshold pixels, the comparative process is performed with the remaining pixels to determine the anomalous pattern in the input medical image.

The threshold pixels PR and PC are responsible for determining the anomaly pattern among the input image pixels by determining the difference among the pixel values. It is notable that the threshold pixels PR and PC are not permanent, and the pair shall be modified based on the search. The major activities of the threshold pixels PR and PC are determining the anomaly pattern pixels, reviewing the anomaly pixels, selecting the surrounding pixels of the anomaly pixels, and classification of the pixels. The basic architecture of the proposed AWDO-based medical image diagnosis is presented in Figure 14.3.

The mathematical models for the pixel analysis for the anomaly behavior, tracking, and the classification process are presented in this section. The parent threshold pixels PR and PC are supported by the other pairs of pixels at various levels, namely different rows and columns. The pixel identification process, determined by the threshold pixels PR and PC, is defined as follows:

(14.1)Pr(n) = |PTR(n)−α×PtR(n)|P⃗(t) − D⃗(t)
(14.2)               PC(n) = |PTC(n)−β×PtC(n)|P⃗(t+1) − D⃗(t+1)

Equations (14.1) and (14.2) represent the target pixels in terms of rows and columns along with the vectors P⃗(t) and D⃗(t). The vectors P⃗(t) and D⃗(t) shall be determined using eqs. (14.3) and (14.4), respectively.

(14.3)$\overrightarrow{P}\left( t \right) = \overset{\rightarrow}{r_{1}}\left( t \right) - 2.\alpha\overset{\rightarrow}{r_{2}}\left( t \right)$
(14.4)$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\overrightarrow{D}\left( t \right) = \overset{\rightarrow}{r_{3}}\left( {t + 1} \right) - 2.\beta\overset{\rightarrow}{r_{4}}\left( {t + 1} \right)$

During the process of iteration, the vectors α and β are chosen randomly in the range of 0 to 1. The terms r1, r2, r3, and r4 are random vectors chosen at random in the range of pixels (0-m) rows and (0-n) columns. The threshold wild dogs (pixels) coordinates in the pixel position (m,n) are used to update the new position of the anomaly pixels in the input medical image. The location of the wild dogs shall be adjusted with the factors α and β in the input medical image. The new locations of the wild dogs in determining the anomaly pattern are represented in eqs. (14.5)–(14.10), respectively.

(14.5)P⃗A(t) = |P⃗(t)−D⃗(t)| × |P⃗(t−1)−D⃗(t−1)| × |P⃗(t+1)−D⃗(t+1)|
(14.6)P⃗A1(t) = |P⃗(t)−D⃗(t)| × α1β1
(14.7)P⃗A2(t) = |P⃗(t−1)−D⃗(t−1)| × α2β2
(14.8)P⃗A3(t) = |P⃗(t+1)−D⃗(t+1)| × α3β3
(14.9) P⃗A4(t) = |P⃗(t−m)−D⃗(t−n)| × α4β4
(14.10)P⃗A5(t) = |P⃗(t+m)−D⃗(t+n)| × α5β5

The P⃗A(t) is the target anomaly pixel, whereas the P⃗A1(t) to P⃗A5(t) is surrounding wild dog pixels are located by the parent threshold pair of the pixels to classify the anomaly pixel. The members of the WDO support the searching process for the anomaly pattern in the input medical image. The vectors P⃗(t) and D⃗(t) are the pairs of hunting dogs that help in attacking the anomaly pixel of the input medical image. The proposed work intentionally employs the two vectors to emphasize exploration and performs the iteration process to determine the anomaly pattern. The movement of the patterns is performed using the two constants, namely α and β, respectively. The targeted pixel undergoes a classification process to determine whether the pixel is infected or normal using the conditional equations (14.11) and (14.12), respectively:

(14.11)If P⃗A(t) ≥ P⃗T(t)
(14.12)If P⃗A(t) < P⃗T(t)

If the pixel value of the target pixel is greater than the pixel value of the threshold pixel, then it is classified as an infected pixel. Otherwise, as represented in eq. (14.12), it is classified as a normal pixel. The AWDO algorithm for performing medical image diagnosis is presented in Table 14.1.

Table 14.1:Algorithm for AWDO in medical image diagnosis.

Algorithm 1: African Wild Dog Optimization (AWDO) in Medical Image Diagnosis
Input: MRI Image (Imxn)
Output: Anomaly Pixel PA(t)
Processes:
1:  Initialize Pixel population:
(14.13)$P_{m \times n} = \frac{d}{dt}\left( I_{m \times n} \right)$

2:  Initialize Threshold Pixel:
(14.14)$P_{T}\left( t \right) = \frac{\int_{i\! = \! 0}^{m}\!{\,\int}_{j\! = \! 0}^{n}\,\,\left( I_{m\! \times \! n} \right)_{ij}dmdn}{\sum_{i\! = \! 0}^{m}\,\,\sum_{j\! = \! 0}^{n}\, M_{i} + N_{j}}$

3: for (i = 0; i++; i = m) && for (j = 0; j++; j = n)

4:
(14.15)Pn(t) = P(t)[i−1;i+2;j−1;j+2].flatten()

5:
(14.16)Pn(t) = Pn*(t)[PnT(t)] = Im × n[i−1;j−1]/​/Pn*(t) =  Neighbor pixel

6:  If; Pn(t) < PT(t);
7:  Return: “Normal Pixel”
8:  Else if Pn(t)≥ PT(t), then
9:  Return, “Infected Pixel”
10: End if
11: End for
12: End processes

The algorithm for the AWDO is illustrated in Table 14.1, which compares the pixel values of the neighboring pixels with the pixel value of the threshold pixel. A greater pixel value results in an infected pixel. The analysis and the comparative analysis are illustrated in the upcoming section.

14.4 Comparative Analysis

The proposed AWDO for determining anomalies in the input multi-modal medical images is analyzed against accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score, and compared with the performance of state-of-the-art methodologies. The performance of the proposed work is compared with state-of-the-art algorithms like support vector machine [21], random forest [22], decision tree [23], particle swarm optimization [24], K-means clustering [25], DNN [26], and recurrent neural networks [27]. The model is trained with the BRATS dataset containing brain tumor images and is tested with images from the same dataset.

The term "accuracy" in terms of medical image diagnostics is considered a critical parameter that assists in determining further treatment. The accuracy is influenced by various parameters like the quality of the input image, tumor heterogeneity, availability of the data, complexity of the algorithm, feature extraction process, and preprocessing algorithm, along with its effectiveness in removing noise from the input test image. The accuracy of the classification is determined in terms of a confusion matrix with true positive (TP), true negative (TN), false positive (FP), and false negative (FN), as depicted in Figure 14.4.

The mathematical representation of the accuracy in terms of the confusion matrix is defined as follows:

(14.17)${Accuracy}\left( A \right) = \frac{TP\, + \, TN}{TP\, + \, TN\, + \, FP\, + \, FN}$

Precision is the performance metric employed to evaluate the quality of the positive predictions made by the proposed classification model. Specifically, precision is the rate at which predictions were made correctly by the classification model. The mathematical representation of precision is defined as follows:

(14.18) ${Precision}\left( P \right) = \frac{TP}{TP\, + \, FP}$

A high precision performance of the classification model indicates that the model is likely to be correct in terms of the classification process. Recall is the alternative parameter for precision, which could be defined as the metric used for determining the actual positive cases that were correctly identified. The term recall can also be termed as sensitivity and is mathematically represented as follows:

(14.19)${Recall}\left( R \right) = \frac{TP}{TP\, + \, FN}$

The recall parameter determines the proportion of actual positive cases that were correctly predicted. The term F1 score is the integrated metric of recall and precision to form a single rate of classification. The F1 score is usually determined to identify the balance between the precision and recall of the classification model. The mathematical representation of the F1 score is defined as follows:

(14.20)$F1\ \,{score\, = \,}\frac{{2\, \times \,}\left( {{Precision\, \times \,}\,{Recall}} \right)}{\left( {{Precision}\,{\, + \,}\,{Recall}} \right)}$

The observed values of the above-mentioned parameters by the state-of-the-art methodologies like support vector machine [21], random forest [22], decision tree [23], particle swarm optimization [24], K-means clustering [25], DNN [26], and recurrent neural networks [27] are listed in Table 14.2.

Table 14.2:Comparison of performance by proposed and state-of-the-art methodologies.

The existing and proposed classification models [28] were trained with the brain tumor datasets, and their accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score are listed in Table 14.2. The graphical comparison is depicted in Figure 14.5.

The proposed model of the AWDO classification algorithm is known for its reduced complexity in terms of performance. In this context, the computational time [29] is measured in the proposed work by providing various types of medical MRI images. Various input images were fed to the proposed model, and the results are depicted in Table 14.3.

The proposed work consumed a maximum of 37.09 µs, which is comparatively minimal compared to the existing state-of-the-art methodologies. The performance analysis proves that the proposed AWDO work demonstrates its supremacy in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score in diagnosing the medical MRI image, along with reduced computational time.

14.5 Conclusion

Medical image diagnosis is a major thrust area and necessitates the incorporation of technology for accurate predictions. Various technologies have been involved in the classification of tumors in various parts of the body and cancer cells, but still experience a major setback in terms of accuracy and consume an enhanced level of computational time. This proposed work employs the AWDO model, which accepts noisy input images and consumes reduced computational time when compared with state-of-the-art methodologies. The AWDO model is designed based on the behavior of the hunting technique employed by African wild dogs. The performance of the proposed AWDO model is compared with existing methodologies, and the results prove that the proposed AWDO model stands ahead in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. In addition, the proposed AWDO model consumes reduced computational complexity. The performance of the proposed AWDO model can further be enhanced with the incorporation of fuzzy logic and rules along with the AWDO model.

15 Artificial Intelligence-Based Control Strategies for COVID-19 That Target Different Age Groups

S. Saranya

Abstract

This chapter describes artificial intelligence (AI) tools in the mathematical model of COVID-19 disease with medication and various methods to control its spread. The age-structured populations’ general MC Kendrick equations are examined to create the model equations utilizing AI approaches to improve the precision and utility of a prey–predator system that pairs one predator with three age groups of prey. AI is useful for accounting for intricate interactions between predators and prey as well as for parameter estimation. We study the equilibria’s existence, positiveness, boundedness, and stability in relation to the inherent carrying capacity of the prey. The primary outcome of this study is the population’s distribution across three age groups and how to prevent disease transmission from predators by using both local and Hopf bifurcation methods. AI models the effects of various public health initiatives like lockdown and social distancing measures to control the spread of the virus. Lastly, the model’s output included numerical examples of Rossler-type AI tools in Maple software.

Keywords: Point of equilibrium, age group targets, Hopf bifurcation, mathematical model of stability switch,

15.1 Introduction

Many of the ideas and principles of the science being discussed are best communicated through mathematical models [17]. With the use of artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, predator–prey relations and rivalry are frequently seen as the two primary obstacles in population models based on mathematics [13, 18]. The behavior of predators and prey can be simulated mathematically to create more accurate predation models. Understanding and modeling the impact of their phenotypic traits require studying how predators and prey respond. Since these models rely heavily on empirical knowledge, they must be compared with the test results gathered in the virtual environment with the individuals present.

The COVID-19 pandemic was first identified in China and rapidly spread to the remainder of the world, leading the World Health Organization to proclaim a worldwide public health emergency. The third respiratory disease outbreak linked to the corona virus in the last 20 years is COVID-19, following Middle East respiratory syndrome and severe acute respiratory syndrome. COVID-19 has devastated the global healthcare system, resulting in thousands of deaths when it first surfaced in Wuhan, China. In the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic, it is critical to identify and screen affected persons as soon as possible because failure to do so could result in the spreading of virus to other people [20]. The actual COVID-19 data is a sequence of observations organized over time, and time-series prediction techniques are well-established in the statistics domain and include structure-based approaches, meta-predictors, and machine learning-based approaches [16].

Data is a fundamental prerequisite for building a framework that the AI community needs to handle this issue. The lack of appropriate data about patients infected with COVID-19 makes it difficult to create identification and analysis models [11]. Due to reluctance among patients to seek medical attention in order to avoid potential confinement, very little information is known about the COVID-19 test-positive patients. Furthermore, some infected individuals do not exhibit any COVID-19 symptoms, making it difficult to pinpoint the exact number of positive cases in large populations [14]. An infected individual becomes more dangerous for others the longer it takes to diagnose them. For this reason, the analysis depends heavily on the availability of vast amounts of data.

Numerous publications examining the impacts of COVID-19 from a statistical, mathematical, and computational standpoint have been released. Susceptible–infectious–recovered is one of the computational frameworks for examining the dynamics of COVID-19 virus. It calculates the spread of an epidemic by taking advantage of a time-dependent system of differential equations [11]. A thorough analysis of the research on predator–prey interactions conducted over the past century reveals how crucial this environment is to understand animal biology’s evolutionary and adaptive processes [18]. Providing for human needs and luxuries continuously depletes the natural world’s ecological balance [3, 7]. The similar underlying methodology based on the aging group population has been utilized in mathematical models to describe the dynamics of diseases [19, 21]. Cushing inquired about numerous formulas for age-structured populations that were obtained from the Mc Kendrick model [15].

After highlighting the three distinct age groups of prey, we can say that:

  1. The age range of the first prey population is from birth to 14 years.

  2. Age range of the second prey population is 15–39 years.

  3. The third age group of prey is those over 40.

Due to their high degree of immunity and implementation of corrective measures, the first and second prey populations will experience a lower incidence of sickness. For the third prey population, which is 40 years of age and over, getting enough nutrients is essential for lowering the danger and severity of viral infections as well as strengthening the defense mechanism. The constant τ is interpreted as a gain in immunity, either through complementary medicine or government-provided vaccinations. In this study, we examine an AI model that simulates the dependence of temporal control measures (facial mask, elbow cough, hand washing, social distancing, and self-quarantine), based on the theory that people infected with COVID-19 can also carelessly transfer the illness [2].

Our primary objectives are: We investigate the optimal performance of AI techniques under the supposition that the control measures (social distancing, face masks, hand washing, elbow coughing, and self-quarantine) limit the infection and the spread of illness. We refer to the continual τ as a natural medicine or vaccination to increase the immune level of prey population, which is people under 40 years old. Distinct prey models are being created, representing distinct physical interactions between prey and predator species, derived from Lotka and Volterra’s groundbreaking work [12, 11]. Here, we are utilizing the carrying capacity for each of the three preys and the control mechanisms for the third prey [3]. We examine the Hopf bifurcation’s direction and stability as it arises at the boundary equilibrium point [9, 14].

This study retrieves the system and solves the guidelines for the system’s local stability [8]. Maintaining the balance of sickness in the prey–predator system is a crucial aspect of the ecosystem for natural coexistence and stability [5, 6]. The results of our investigation into how three preys interact with a single predator model under varying incidences and disease-related mortality rates including vaccination and natural medicine are highlighted [2, 16]. Lastly, we display the numerical solution findings for every model at different parameter values. Symbolic computation and algebra, machine learning integration, natural language processing, predictive analysis, and other AI technologies are used in Maple 15 programming.

15.2 Technique for Choosing Values for Parameters

Three prey population subpopulations, shown by three prey populations, are created by the model from the whole population as N1(t), N2(t), N3(t) at time t, and one predator population N4(t). Examine the 4D model system as follows:

$\ \frac{dN_{1}}{dt} = aN_{1}\left( {1 - \frac{N_{1}\ }{k_{1}}} \right) - \alpha\ N_{1}N_{4}$
$\ \frac{dN_{2}}{dt} = bN_{2}\left( {1 - \frac{N_{2}\ }{k_{2}}} \right) - \beta\ N_{2}N_{4}$
$\ \frac{dN_{3}}{dt} = cN_{3}\left( {1 - \frac{N_{3}\ }{k_{3}}} \right) - \gamma\ N_{3}N_{4} - eN_{3} + U\tau N_{3}$
(15.1)$\ \frac{dN_{4}}{dt} = \eta\ N_{1}N_{4} + \delta\ N_{2}N_{4} + \mu\ N_{3}N_{4} - f\,{\! N_{4}}$

with initial conditions

(15.2)Nl(t) ≥ 0, N2(t) ≥ 0, N3(t) ≥ 0, N4(t) ≥ 0

The first, second, third, and predator are denoted by the parameters N1(t), N2(t), N3(t), and N4(t), respectively, and may be found in this case. Here is a description of the model parameters:

The first, second, and third prey’s respective specific growth rates are a, b, c.

The corresponding carrying capabilities of the first, second, and third preys are k1, k2, k3.

The predator interacts with three preys (N1, N2, N3) in the following ways: α, β, and γ.

e is the third prey population’s natural death. U represents the control shown in Figure 15.1. τ denotes the increased immunity with the intake of natural medicines.

The conversion factors for predators from the three prey populations are η, δ, and μ.

The natural death of the predator is f.

This model includes certain assumptions, consisting of:

  1. In the first, second, and third prey populations, interactions occur through predators.

  2. Strong immune growth from infancy to 39 years allows the first and second prey populations to recover after interactions with predators.

  3. Three populations of prey possessing carrying capacities and intrinsic growth rates of a, b, and c and k1, k2, k3  were fitted using the Leslie–Gower model, and no interaction was found between them.

  4. The virus only affects one-third of the prey population, as immunity develops and dies naturally. Also, we raise the immunity growth by AI through parameter estimation, such as constants Uτ, where U is the control measure (see Figure 4.1) and τ is the immunization or alternative medicine:

    τ = cardamom, ginger, turmeric, cumin seeds, and pepper

  5. After implementing control measures like Uτ, the afflicted prey recovers in a third prey population as a result of higher immune growth.

  6. Predators are weakened in primary and secondary prey populations, but not in tertiary prey populations.

15.3 Boundedness and Positivity of the Specified System

15.3.1 Positivity

Theorem 15.1: The given equation system (1) is never negative. Therefore, every potential outcome for system (15.1) is positive.

Proof.

Given that system (15.1)’s right-hand side is locally Lipschitzian on C and entirely continuous, condition (15.2) is distinct on [0, ξ), where 0 < ξ ≤ +∞ as in [16]. With initial conditions (15.2) applied to system (15.1), we have

$N_{1}\left( t \right) = N_{1}\left( 0 \right)\exp\left\lbrack {\int\left\{ {a\left( {1 - \!\frac{N_{1}\left( t \right)}{k_{1}}} \right) - \alpha N_{4}\left( t \right)} \right\} dt} \right\rbrack\! > {}0$
$N_{2}\left( t \right) = N_{2}\left( 0 \right)\exp\left\lbrack {\int\left\{ {b\left( {1 - \!\frac{N_{2}\left( t \right)}{k_{2}}} \right) - \beta N_{4}\left( t \right)} \right\} dt} \right\rbrack\! > {}0$
$N_{3}\left( t \right) = N_{3}\left( 0 \right)\exp\left\lbrack {\int\left\{ {c\left( {1 - \!\frac{N_{3}\left( t \right)}{k_{3}}} \right) - \gamma N_{4}\left( t \right) + U\tau} \right\} dt} \right\rbrack\! > {}0$
N4(t) = N4(0)exp [∫{ηN1(t)+δN2(t)+μN3(t)−f}dt]​ > 0

which brings the proof to an end.

15.4.2 Analysis of Stability and Existence of Equilibrium Points

The existence and stability behavior of system (15.1) at the equilibrium locations are examined in this section [10]:

  • The trivial equilibrium point E1 is a saddle point.

  • The axial equilibrium points E3 and E5 are saddle points.

  • The planar equilibrium points E4 and E6 are saddle points.

  • The planar equilibrium of E2, E11, E13, and E14 is unstable.

  • The planar equilibrium of E7, E8, E9, E10, and E12 are asymptotically stable locally. The equilibrium points E7, E8, E9, E10, E12, and the internal equilibrium point E15 will be interpreted.

  • At equilibrium, the Jacobian matrix of system (15.1) will interpret the equilibrium points E7, E8, E9, E10, E12, and the interior equilibrium point E15.

System (15.1)’s equilibrium point Jacobian matrix E = (N1(t),N2(t),N3(t),N4(t)) is given by

J = [m11 0 0−N1α 0 m22 0−N2β o 0 m33−N3γ N4η N4δ N4μ m44]

where $m_{11} = a - 2\frac{a\ N_{1}\ }{\ k_{1}} - N_{4}\alpha,\ m_{22} = b - 2\frac{b\ N_{2}\ }{\ k_{2}} - N_{4}\beta,\ m_{33} = c - 2\frac{c\ N_{3}\ }{\ k_{3}} - N_{4}\gamma - e + U\tau$, m44 = N1η + N2δ + N3μ − f.

Due to the nature of the eigenvalues, eq. (15.1) is stable if all eigenvalues are negative for the real roots of the Jacobian characteristic equation above, and have negative real parts for the complex roots. Otherwise, the system will become unstable.

15.5 Hopf bifurcation

The Hopf bifurcation around the interior equilibrium point E15 was studied in this section. The bifurcation parameter N3 is identified by the basic parameter c, which represents the prey’s growth rate. The Jacobian matrix JE15 experiences Hopf bifurcation, wherein two of its eigenvalues are solely imaginary, while the remaining eigenvalues containing non-positive real components are  Re[dλ/dc]|c = c0 ≠ 0[4]. Assume that the interior equilibrium point’s characteristic equation E15 is as follows:

(15.3)λ4 + A3λ3 + A2λ2 + A1λ1 + A0 = 0

The characteristic polynomial coefficients (15.3) meet the following requirement for just imaginary eigenvalues A3A2A1 − A32A0 − A12 = 0.

Assume that ±iω represents two purely imaginary eigenvalues that match c0. From the characteristic equation (15.3),

$\left\lbrack {4\lambda^{3} + 3A_{3}\lambda^{2} + 2A_{2}\lambda + A_{1}} \right\rbrack\ \frac{d\lambda}{dc} + \left( {\lambda^{3}\frac{dA}{dc} + \lambda^{2}\frac{dA}{dc} + \lambda\frac{dA}{dc} + \frac{dA}{dc}} \right) = 0$

Hence

(15.4)$\frac{d\lambda}{dc} = \! - \!\left( \frac{\lambda^{3}\ \frac{dA}{dc} + \lambda^{2}\ \frac{dA}{dc} + \lambda\ \frac{dA}{dc} + \frac{dA}{dc}}{4\lambda^{3} + 3A_{3}\lambda^{2} + 2A_{2}\lambda + A_{1}} \right)$

When we change iω in eq. (15.4), we get

$\ \frac{d\lambda}{dc}|_{i\omega} = \! - \!\left( \frac{- i\omega^{3}\ \frac{dA_{3}}{dc} - \frac{\omega^{2}dA_{2}}{dc} + \frac{i\omega dA_{1}}{dc} + \frac{dA_{0}}{dc}}{- 4i\omega^{3} - 3A_{3}\omega^{2} + 2A_{2}i\omega + A_{1}} \right)$

Hence ${Re}\left( {\frac{d\lambda}{dc}|_{i\omega}} \right) = - \left( \frac{\left\lbrack {A - 3A_{3}\omega^{2}} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack {\frac{dA_{0}}{dc} - \omega^{2}\frac{dA_{2}}{dc}} \right\rbrack + \left\lbrack {2A_{2}\omega - 4\omega^{3}} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack {\omega^{3}\frac{dA_{3}}{dc} - \omega\frac{dA_{1}}{dc}} \right\rbrack}{{\lbrack A_{1} - 3A_{3}\omega^{2}\rbrack}^{2} + \left\lbrack {2A_{2}\omega - 4\omega^{3}} \right\rbrack^{2}} \right)$

Theorem 15.15: If we assume that “c” is the bifurcation parameter, then system (1) maintains the given Hopf bifurcation $\left( {\left\lbrack {A_{1} - 3A_{3}\omega^{2}} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack {\frac{dA_{0}}{dc} - \omega^{2}\frac{dA_{2}}{dc}} \right\rbrack + \left\lbrack {2A_{2}\omega - 4\omega^{3}} \right\rbrack\!\,\left\lbrack {\omega^{3}\frac{dA_{3}}{dc} - \omega\frac{dA_{1}}{dc}} \right\rbrack} \right) \neq 0.$

15.7 Discussions and Conclusions

There are some quite intriguing dynamics in an eco-epidemiology model with three prey and one predator as the sickness spreads to the third prey group. In this case, we imagined that all three preys develop logistically, with the exception of the third, which is incapable of procreating. Therefore, with the use of Maple and AI approaches, all of our significant analytical discoveries are quantitatively validated. The time-delayed system experiences a Hopf bifurcation at approximately E* at c = c*, taking time delay c as the bifurcation parameter.

Finally, take some control measure Uτ, which plays an important role in controlling population stability. This model will analyze the stability, which is shown in Table 15.1:

  • From Figure 15.2, we observed that the first prey N1 belongs to the child age increases and becomes constant, and the second prey N2 belongs to adult age and becomes constant due to lower immunity growth compared to the first prey.

  • From Figure 15.3, we find that the first prey N1 and second prey N2 becomes constant, but the third prey N3 increases slowly because of infection by the predator N4.

  • From Figure 15.4, we have shown that the third prey N3 increases because of the control measure Uτ acting as a key role but the predator N4 decreases.

  • From Figure 15.5, we find that the second prey N2 goes to a constant, while the predator N4 decreases.

  • From Figure 15.6, we observe that the first prey N1 increases and then becomes constant, while the predator N4 decreases.

  • From Figure 15.7, we find that the first prey N1 and the second prey N2 become a constant, and the third prey N3 increases because of the parameter value of the control measure Uτ = 0.58315 so as to avoid the disease from spreading, while the predator N4 diminishes instantly.

In our real-life situations, we compare this model by following the constant mentioned in Uτ as a preventive way to avoid the disease from spreading. Therefore, to avoid the spread of infection and disease, the predator spread in a third prey population could be reduced by applying the prevention and control measures described in Figure 15.1, as τ control is recommended.

16 Model Optimization in Deep Learning: Theory and Application

Neha
Shailja
Umesh Kumar Lilhore

Abstract

Model optimization is the most important component in the deep learning field, impacting performance and model training. In this chapter, techniques of optimization and their theoretical and practical implementations will be discussed. We will focus on the optimization techniques used in deep learning, which improve the accuracy of the model, convergence speed, and efficiency. Optimization techniques such as stochastic gradient descent and its variants, including momentum, RMSProp, and Adam, are explored in depth. Different types of optimizers will be used for updating the learning rate to minimize the objective function. Some advanced optimization methods, such as adaptive learning and gradient clipping, have been discussed in depth. A comparative analysis of variants of gradient descent and various other optimizers will be discussed, highlighting the important features.

Keywords: Optimization algorithm, stochastic gradient descent, momentum, RMSProp, Adam optimizer,

16.1 Basic theory

Deep learning (DL) is a powerful machine learning (ML) technique that can learn through data patterns and enhance functions by repeatedly examining algorithms. In DL, optimization plays a significant role in enhancing the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) models. Model optimization provides a foundation for DL by introducing an iterative method of adjusting model features (such as weights and biases) to minimize the error rate and enhance the accuracy of the model. It generates a high-dimensional parameter space that results in the most accurate predictions on given problems related to classification, regression, or the generation of new data. The most important features of optimization are hyperparameter tuning, in which the rate of learning, size of batch, and the count of layers are used to achieve optimal performance [1].

Techniques of regularization like L2 regularization are used to avoid overfitting and also help in improving the ability of the model to specify the unseen data. Some more methods used to minimize the size and computational requirements of the model are pruning and quantization. In DL, pruning is used to build a neural network model that is small in size and more effective [2]. The objective of pruning is to remove the unwanted neurons and connections so that we can get a cost-effective model that takes less training time. Quantization methods are used to shrink the weights of neurons to one-fourth of the original weight to improve the performance of the model. The main objective of optimizers in DL is to develop models whose accuracy is high as well as more effective and scalable. This chapter tries to bridge the gap between theoretical aspects and practical implementations, providing a thorough understanding of various optimization techniques and their relevance to DL [3].

16.2 Fundamentals of optimization

Optimization techniques are most widely used in the field of ML as well as DL. These are used to learn about the parameters of the data taken as input. Hence, optimization techniques provide the successful execution of results to real-world problems. Various researches have been directed to find out the best algorithms for the problems to give the best solution, as there is no particular method that can solve various types of problems [3]. In this chapter, various optimization algorithms will be discussed like all the variants of gradient descent (GD) such as stochastic GD (SGD) and mini-batch GD (MBGD). Both differ based on the size of data used for calculating the learning rate and also for training DL models. The biggest challenge faced by the optimizer is how to select the varying learning rate [2]. Many optimizers will be discussed to overcome the challenges. The key elements of optimization algorithms are summarized in Table 16.1.

Table 16.1:Elements of optimization algorithms.

Keyword Description
Gradient descent Optimizer for finding the minimum of a function
Learning rate A hyperparameter that controls how much to adjust the weights of our network with respect to the loss gradient
Batch size The number of training samples used for an iteration
Epoch One iteration through the whole training dataset
Overfitting After training on data, when the model fits too well, it results in overfitting
Loss function A function that measures how well the model’s predictions match the actual data
Backpropagation The gradient of the function is calculated with respect to weights
Hyperparameters Parameters that are set before the learning process starts and control the process of training

16.2.1 Elements of optimization algorithms

16.2.1.1 Hyperparameters

Hyperparameters are the most significant component used in the optimization of DL and ML models. As parameters used in the model are identified during training, hyperparameters are identified before the process of training starts. Some common approaches used for selecting hyperparameters are grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization. Hyperparameters need to be chosen carefully for the best results [4].

16.2.1.2 Backpropagation

Backpropagation means backward propagation of errors. It is a method that is used to minimize the error in a neural network. Backpropagation is the most vital algorithm used in neural network optimization, which enables them to acquire from data by modifying weights and biases. It helps in minimizing the overall error. Some of the basic key concepts used in backpropagation are forward pass, loss function, and backward pass [5].

16.2.1.3 Loss Function

In the field of DL, a loss function measures the difference between the output predicted by the model and the original data. It is also known as an objective function or cost function. There are various optimizers used to minimize the loss function for improving the performance of the model. Some of the commonly used loss functions are mean squared error, mean absolute error, and so on [6].

16.2.1.4 Overfitting

Overfitting means that while training, the model learns from so much data, including noise, resulting in learning some patterns that are not relevant with respect to the data. Because of this, the model becomes too complex and fits so well that it captures not only the correct patterns but also random fluctuations and outliers. It leads to high accuracy. To reduce overfitting in the model, we can improve the quality of data by removing unimportant features, extracting meaningful patterns, and mitigating the risk of fitting the noise or features that are not relevant [7].

16.3 Optimizers in deep learning

16.3.1 Gradient-Based Optimization Methods

GD is measured as the most important concept of optimization in DL. This method uses mathematical concepts to update the value and achieve the local minima, as shown in Figure 16.1. When the model is trained by GD in DL, a step size has to be selected, that is, alpha. The most common problem faced by everyone is choosing the best value of alpha. If the value of alpha is too small, then the performance of the optimizer is very slow, and if it is too big, the optimizer fails to converge. To find the optimal alpha value, we need to find the derivative of the objective function with respect to alpha, as well [8]:

(16.1)y_new = y − alpha*f(x)

Here in eq. (16.1), y is the current value, alpha represents the learning rate, and f(x) is the derivative of the function at y. The above equation is used to calculate gradient. In this, alpha is used to denote the step size, which means how far to travel with each gradient for every iteration [9].

Following is the step-by-step working of GD:

  1. At first, we will begin with the starting coefficients.

  2. Then calculate the cost of coefficients and find out which has the lesser cost compared to the current one.

  3. We move towards the lower weight and modify the coefficient's value.

  4. Repeat this process iteratively.

  5. The process will be repeated until the local minimum point is reached. A local minimum is a point beyond which it cannot proceed.

The GD algorithm works best for convex functions but not for non-convex functions. To overcome the problem of GD when dealing with large datasets, there are many ways to address this using various types of optimization algorithms.

Generally, there are three types of GD:

  1. SGD

  2. BGD (batch GD)

  3. MBGD

Every type of GD is differentiated based on the size of data used to calculate the gradient of the loss or minimum function, the accuracy of the coefficient updates, and the time taken for updating the coefficients (Figure 16.2) [1]. For a detailed comparison of BGD, MBGD, and SGD, refer to Table 16.2.

16.3.1.1 Stochastic Gradient Descent

The SGD optimizer is an important optimization algorithm in ML as well as in the DL field, especially for big datasets. It is an iterative method that modifies the values by considering steps proportional to the gradient of the loss function. SGD calculates the gradient based on an individual random data point or a small part of the dataset at each iteration, as shown in Figure 16.3. This randomness allows for the selection of data batches, reducing the need for large datasets and significant computational time [10].

The SGD optimizer is ideal for DL with massive data and significant computational time [10]. So, we can say that in DL, mostly the SGD optimizer is preferred when the size of the data is too large, and it provides efficient computational time. The update rule is similar to GD as follows:

(16.2)ynew = y − alpha*f(x)

16.3.1.2 Batch Gradient Descent (BGD)

Batch gradient descent (BGD) is also called vanilla gradient descent, which is used to calculate the gradient of the cost function for the complete dataset [9, 10]. In this method, the gradient is calculated for the complete dataset, as shown in Figure 16.4, to make just one update of parameters, as follows:

(16.3)y = y − η*∇Z(y)

where

  • y: Model features

  • η: Learning rate

  • ∇Z(y): Gradient of the cost function J with respect to θ.

16.3.1.3 Mini-Batch Gradient Descent

This is the another most widely used variant of gradient descent known as mini-batch. In this method, the breakdown of a large dataset is done into small batches, as shown in Figure 16.5, and after every batch, the value of the model's parameters is updated, ensuring global minima in fewer steps [11, 12].

The advantage of a mini-batch optimizer is the use of less memory and low variance in the model. MBGD inherits features from both SGD and vanilla gradient descent (BGD). This can help in reducing noise in the update of model parameters and improve convergence [13, 14].

Table 16.2:Comparison of gradient descent methods.

Feature BGD SGD MBGD
Data used Entire dataset Single data point Small subset (batch) of data
Gradient calculation Calculated on entire dataset Calculated on a single data point Calculated on a batch of data
Convergence Slower, but more stable Faster, but less stable Faster than BGD, more stable than SGD
Computational cost High Low Medium
Memory usage High Low Medium
Risk of local minima Lower Higher Medium
Typical use cases Smaller datasets and convex problems Large datasets and online learning The most common balance is between BGD and SGD

16.3.2 Momentum-Based Optimizer

As we have already discussed about GD optimization algorithms, the standard SGD optimizer requires a greater number of iterations to achieve lower minima due to the noisy process. Computational speed suffers as a result. A momentum approach is applied to solve this problem, aiding in the loss function’s faster convergence. This algorithm modifies weights based on oscillations in the gradient direction [14, 15].

It can, however, go more quickly if a small portion of the prior update is added. It is necessary to remember that a high momentum phase should be used to lower the learning rate. This method is based on the last value, learning rate, and a new parameter is added as gamma, which is used to control this history update. The update rule for a momentum-based optimizer will be like y = y – v, where v is the history element [16, 17], as follows:

(16.4)v = gamma*v + alpha*f′(a)
(16.5)y_new = a − v

16.3.3 Nesterov accelerated gradient (NAG)

NAG is one of the most widely used optimization techniques, which is based on the classical momentum approach in GD. While the momentum method focuses on the historical values for the update of parameters, the NAG technique focuses on the “look-ahead” mechanism. In this mechanism, before calculating the gradient, the algorithm predicts the future positions of the model parameters based on the momentum [18] as follows:

(16.6)vt = γvt − 1 + η∇θJ(θ−γvt−1)
(16.7)yt = gamma*yt − 1 + alpha∇ θJ (θ−gamma*yt​−​1)

Here yt is the momentum, alpha is the learning rate, and θJ(θ–gamma✶y_(t–1) = gradient of the objective function.

Now, we can say that we are able to modify the error function with the help of history and next values, which results in speeding up the convergence by using the NAG technique [18].

16.3.4 Adagrad (Adaptive Gradient Descent)

As in the above algorithms, the same learning rate was updated for all the parameters; the adaptive GD algorithm changes the training parameters to use different learning rates for each iteration based on differences in training parameters. The Adagrad optimizer directs to provide an adaptive learning rate by declining the learning rate proportional to the modified gradient history. The only negative of this technique is that the learning rate falls violently, ultimately approaching zero. The advantage of using Adagrad is that it eliminates the need to modify the learning rate manually [19].

Calculate the squared gradient by using eq. (16.8) and update the parameters as follows:

(16.8)G = G + f′(y)2

Update parameters calculated by using the following equation:

(16.9)$y\_{ne}{w_{= \frac{a - {alpha}}{\sqrt{G + {epsilon}}}}}^{\ast}f^{\prime}\left( y \right)$

In this approach, the learning rate is not modified manually. The Adagrad approach is used more compared to other GD variants. Sometimes the learning rate becomes too slow, which causes the model to be unable to gain more knowledge and results in less accuracy of the model [20].

16.3.5 RMSProp

Root mean square propagation, or RMSProp, is an optimizer algorithm similar to the Adagrad approach. Although it has not been published, the concept of this approach is well-known in the community. It focuses on solving the problem of fluctuating gradients. In other optimizers, the value of the gradient keeps changing; sometimes it is very small, and sometimes it is very large. This problem cannot be solved with an individual learning rate. This optimizer is a progression of the Adagrad optimizer, as it reduces the repetitive decrease in the learning rate [21]. RMSProp can be measured by the following equations:

(16.10)E[g∧​2)_t = 0.9*E[g∧2)_{t−1} + 0.1*g_t∧2
(16.11)a_new  = a − alpha/ sqrt(E[g∧2)_t+epsilon)*g_t

16.3.6 Adaptive moment estimation (Adam)

Adaptive moment estimation optimizer is an optimization algorithm used in the field of DL. It is an advancement of the SGD optimization algorithm and is used to modify the weights during the process of training in a neural network. This is also known as the Adam optimizer. This combines the important features of Adagrad and RMSProp. The Adam optimizer calculates the learning rate for individual data considering the history of gradients and their second moment [20, 21]. By calculating the mean (first moment) and uncentred variance (second moment), this optimizer gets an adaptive learning rate, resulting in speeding up convergence and better performance of the neural network [22]. As presented in Table 16.3, each optimization algorithm has distinct advantages and drawbacks depending on the problem context.

Table 16.3:Comparison of different optimization algorithms, highlighting features, advantages, and disadvantages.

Optimizer Key features Advantages Drawbacks
SGD (stochastic gradient descent) Weights are updated with the help of gradients Simple and easy to implement Can be slow to converge and may get stuck in local minima; sensitive to the learning rate
Momentum Add the last update to the current Accelerates convergence May overshoot the minimum if the momentum is too high
Nesterov accelerated gradient (NAG) Look-ahead approach is used for calculating the gradient at the anticipated future position Improves upon momentum by anticipating updates, which can lead to faster convergence Similar issues arise with momentum, as it is sensitive to learning rate and momentum parameters
Adagrad Adjusts the learning rate based on the frequency of parameter updates; accumulates squared gradients Suitable for sparse data, it performs well on problems with sparse features Learning rate decreases over time, potentially becoming too small for further training
RMSProp The moving average of squared gradients is used to scale the learning rate Prevents rapid decrease in learning rate and stabilizes training Requires careful tuning of the decay rate; it may perform poorly on some non-stationary tasks
Adam (adaptive moment estimation) Combines the benefits of Adagrad and RMSProp, maintaining a per-parameter learning rate and momentum Adaptive learning rates and momentum help in faster convergence and handling sparse gradients May not generalize well under some conditions; sensitive to hyperparameter tuning

16.4 Applications of Optimization in Various Fields

16.4.1 Engineering and Operations Research

16.4.1.1 Structural Optimization

In engineering design, structural optimization is used to enhance the performance of structures like bridges and buildings. Topology optimization is a process that focuses on optimal material layout, finding the best distribution of material to maximize structural efficiency. Structural optimization is used in various fields to improve performance and resource utilization, including aerospace, automotive, and civil engineering [22].

16.4.1.2 Supply Chain Optimization

In supply chain network design, optimization plays an important role in determining the best locations for warehouses, cost reduction, and inventory management. Complex problems can be resolved with the use of mathematical programming and heuristic techniques, resulting in reliable answers with practical applications. Better resource use, more efficient operations, and heightened market competition are the outcomes of this optimization [23].

16.4.1.3 Production Planning

Optimizers are used to design production schedules that are effective. This involves determining start and end times, assigning jobs to machines, and considering factors like machine capacity and due dates. The aim is to minimize production time, costs, or other relevant metrics [24].

16.4.2 Machine Learning

16.4.2.1 Neural Network Training

Millions of parameters are usually used to train a neural network. The main objective of the optimizers (such as GD) is to adjust these parameters to minimize the error between the network’s predictions and the actual data. GD uses an iterative approach in ML and DL, where it is used to minimize error functions [25].

16.4.2.2 Hyperparameter Tuning

ML models have settings called hyperparameters, and finding the optimal hyperparameter values is also a challenge that significantly impacts performance. Bayesian optimization is a powerful technique to find optimal values. Therefore, optimizers can automatically find the best combination of hyperparameters to achieve the desired outcome [26].

16.4.3 Finance

16.4.3.1 Portfolio Optimization and Risk management

Optimizers are also helpful in creating investment portfolios by optimizing asset allocation based on statistical measures of risk and return. Financial institutions use optimizers to assess and manage risks. Techniques like value at risk help quantify potential losses, and optimizers can be used to find strategies to mitigate these risks [27].

16.4.4 Other Fields

16.4.4.1 Healthcare

By identifying substances with specific characteristics, optimizers are used to create novel pharmaceuticals. One popular method used by optimizers to forecast a molecule’s affinity for a target protein is called molecular docking [28, 29].

16.4.4.2 Robotics

In robotics, the models use optimizers to plan effective routes, avoid obstacles, and carry out jobs as efficiently as possible. They are employed in many different applications, including autonomous cars and industrial robots.

16.5 Challenges in optimization techniques

As optimization techniques are used by various fields to make models more efficient and effective, they also come with several challenges. These challenges can range from the complexity of data, changes in constraints, dynamic environments, and many other problems listed below:

  1. Scalability: When the size of the problem increases, many optimization problems become difficult computationally. This becomes particularly difficult for combinatorial optimization problems, where the number of possible solutions grows exponentially.

  2. Non-convexity: Finding the global optimum in non-convex problems is challenging because traditional optimization methods can get stuck in local optima, as non-convexity is a situation where a single function has more than one local minimum and there is no guarantee of a unique optimal solution [8].

  3. High Dimensionality: Optimization problems with a large number of variables can be an issue due to the effect of dimensionality. The search space increases exponentially with the number of dimensions, making it harder to identify the optimal solution.

  4. Data Quality and Availability: The main factor in the efficiency of optimization techniques is the availability and accuracy of data. Incomplete, incorrect, or noisy data can result in wrong results.

  5. Algorithm Selection and Computational Resources: The performance of the model also depends on algorithm selection. Therefore, choosing the right optimization algorithm is also a challenge. Along with this, proper computational power and sufficient time are required by some optimization algorithms, which is sometimes not possible in real-life applications.

  6. Interpretability and Implementation: Even if an optimal solution is found, it must be interpretable and implementable in practice. A complex algorithm includes complex calculations, formulas, and variables, which make them difficult to understand. Therefore, even if a solution is mathematically optimal, it may face problems if it is not understandable or actionable by the client [30].

16.6 Conclusion

In this chapter, we focus on the fundamentals of optimization and various types of optimizers. The optimization techniques play a vital role in training DL models. This chapter focuses on updating the learning rate in different ways to minimize the loss function using optimizers such as variants of DG, momentum, Adam, RMSProp, Adagrad, and NAG. There are many aspects and features that can be considered, such as the nature of the problem, the size of the data for training, and hyperparameter sensitivity for selecting the most suitable optimizer for performing the task. This also focuses on the comparison of different optimizers, highlighting the features of every optimizer.

There are many challenges faced by optimizers, such as algorithm selection, data quality, and scalability. Optimizers are used in various fields like healthcare, engineering, finance, machine learning, and robotics. The research is still ongoing to improve optimization algorithms, which will be helpful in increasing the performance of DL models.
