19 Principles and Applications of Bayesian Optimization in AI

Dankan Gowda V
Anand Polamarasetti
Pullela S. V. V. S. R. Kumar
Aparna Atul Junnarkar
Bhaskar Roy

Abstract

This chapter focuses on understanding the Bayesian optimization (BO) method and its use in the context of artificial intelligence (AI) with the aim of intelligently solving expensive problems. Thus, BO is now an important tool for improving different AI applications, including hyperparameter optimization in machine learning models, neural architecture search, and reinforcement learning. By using probabilistic models like Gaussian processes, BO is efficient when it comes to exploitation and exploration, therefore making it possible to arrive at an optimal solution within a few evaluations. This chapter further elaborates on other mathematical concepts in BO, such as surrogate modeling, acquisition functions, and the exploration–exploitation dilemma. It also provides examples of real problems that exemplify how BO can be helpful in increasing accuracy, speed, and reducing computational time when used in applications such as autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and robotics. Some of these challenges include scalability issues and computational burdens, as well as some future research and development areas. This brief survey, therefore, underscores the application of BO in the likely radical revolution of AI and how this innovation is critical for the progressive development of intelligent systems.

Keywords: Bayesian optimization, artificial intelligence, surrogate models, acquisition functions, hyperparameter tuning, neural architecture search, reinforcement learning, optimization techniques, machine learning, AI performance, real-time applications,

19.1 Introduction

19.1.1 Overview of Bayesian Optimization (BO)

Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sequential design strategy to optimize the expensive black-box functions. Unlike other optimization methods that may take a number of function evaluations, BO constructively models the objective function through the process of search space exploration. Normally, the use of Gaussian processes (GP) as a surrogate model to represent the unknown function is preferred since it not only provides the prediction but also the uncertainty related to the prediction [1]. This probabilistic approach allows BO to explore and exploit new points effectively, which makes the algorithm useful in any scenario where the evaluation of the objective function is either complex or time-consuming. In artificial intelligence (AI), these evaluations can consist of the training of large sophisticated machine learning models, setting hyperparameters or perhaps setting up reinforcement learning policies [2]. BO’s major benefit is its sample efficiency, that is, achieving near optimality with as few evaluations as possible, which helps to save significant computational costs.

19.1.2 Importance of Optimization in AI

Different stages of AI are influenced by optimization, especially when developing or implementing machine learning models. Now, at the center of nearly every AI system, there is the idea of optimizing some kind of objective function, which can often mean accuracy, loss, and so on [3]. For instance, in supervised learning, the optimization part entails the finding of new parameters for a model that will lower the loss function, thus making the model more capable of predicting or classifying new data. Optimization is also central to hyperparameter tuning, which is another important aspect that cannot afford to be without optimization [4]. The efficacy of pursuing machine learning depends on factors such as learning rates, regularization conditions, and the type of network. Several older approaches such as grid search or even random search are not efficient and are rather time-consuming as the number of hyperparameters increases [5]. Unlike grid search, BO is better because it can determine which couple of hyperparameters to assess next, thereby improving the rate of finding the best configurations.

Optimization is another field that is relevant in areas such as neural network architecture search and is based on the search for the optimal architecture among a huge number of possible designs [6]. This task is by its nature nontrivial, especially due to the fact that it operates within a high-dimensional space. BO, being capable of efficiently optimizing large and complex search spaces, has proved beneficial in finding architectures that produce high performance [7]. Likewise, in reinforcement learning, for which the aim is to enhance the policy for the maximization of accrued reward, BO is useful for picking policy parameters or designing reward functions for a better learning process [8]. These different forms of optimization highlight how versatile BO is in tackling challenges that are diverse in nature, making it extremely crucial in bolstering development in AI.

Figure 19.1 presents the flow of BO, also known as the sequential design, which outlines the iterative optimization process of an expensive-to-optimize objective function. Shown in this figure is that the optimization first starts with the choice of a few initial sample points on which the GP surrogate model of the objective function is constructed [9]. The mean of the actual surrogate model is the equivalent of what it currently knows, while the confidence interval is the degree of uncertainty it holds. Another function that is employed in the selection process is an acquisition function, say, expected improvement (EI), with which one can select the next sample point with respect to exploration and exploitation [10]. This point is then assessed against the actual objective function, and the outcome is then fed back into the GP model. This means the process continues in this manner with many iterations until a certain criterion that can be set by the programmer is met. In this way, the proficiency of BO in finding the best solution in the quickest way is evident.

The optimization accomplishment with regard to function value and time taken is presented in Figure 19.2, which consists of BO, grid search, and random search [11]. The plot on the right depicts the objective function measure against the number of function evaluations, which provides information on the convergence rate of each method to the optimal solution. From the results of Figure 19.2, it can be observed that BO achieves higher values near the true optimum, as opposed to algorithms like grid search and random search that require a relatively higher number of evaluations to reach a similar level of true optimum [12]. This figure also illustrates how the use of BO, in comparison with the other methods, is computationally less time-consuming and provides better results in terms of optimization speed and quality of the acquired solutions. This states the fact that if function evaluations are costly or require much time, then this is the most appropriate approach to such problems.

19.1.3 Purpose and Scope of the Chapter

The main goal of this chapter is twofold: first, to provide the reader with the necessary understanding of BO; second, to present three instances of usage of BO in AI. Thus, when working through the theoretical elements like surrogate modeling with GPs or the definition of the acquisition functions, this chapter is supposed to give a clear background on how BO works [13]. BO also goes through real-life examples where BO can be used to improve machine learning models, adjust their parameters, perform neural architecture search, and come up with better ways of learning in reinforcement learning [14]. These applications will be discussed in detail with the help of examples in order to demonstrate how BO can be used in different AI scenarios [15]. In addition, the chapter will also elaborate on the limitations as well as future prospects of BO while highlighting this research. Leaving the chapter, readers will be familiar with how BO can be applied to enhance AI systems, which will be resourceful for persons intending to develop the field [16]. This extensive review serves as the platform to propose the utilization of BO for the resolution of challenging AI problems in practice that have not seen a concrete application so far.

19.2 Principles of Bayesian Optimization

19.2.1 Mathematical foundation

BO relies on the construction and repeated improvement of a probabilistic model of the objective function; hence, it can be very useful for expensive or noisy functions. It is also important that some concepts of BO are based on two key mathematical tools: GPs and acquisition functions [17]. The information, which is the goal function, can be modeled with the help of GPs because they are flexible and able to estimate uncertainty [18]. A GP is a stochastic model for functions that captures the full distribution over functions characterized by mean and covariance functions, giving the measure of similarity between points in the input space.

Mathematically, a GP can be represented as follows:

f(x)  ∼  GP(m(x),k(x,x′))

where m(x) is the mean function, which is often assumed to be zero for simplicity, and k(x,x′) is the covariance function, which determines the shape and smoothness of the function being modeled [19]. With prior knowledge and by updating this model with the observed data, GPs regulate the objective function prediction at any point along with the certainty of it.

Figure 19.3 illustrates the mapping of the GP model on BO as a surrogate model. The figure combines the actual objective function, the mean prediction of the GP, and the intervals of uncertainty [20]. It also demonstrates the method by which the GP model employs initial sample points to return uncertainty estimates of the objective function [21]. The confidence intervals shed light on which areas are characterized by a high level of uncertainty and are therefore used to select new sample points [22]. It can be seen from this figure that the surrogate model fits the objective function for the approximations and uses uncertainty as an important factor in determining the optimization process, which plays an important role in exploring the search space in BO.

Figure 19.4 shows the acquisition function based on the EI criterion. The figure adds the acquisition function to the GP surrogate model, mean prediction, and standard deviation. It illustrates how the acquisition function is used to decide where to sample next by incorporating the mean and variance [23]. The EI function recommends points with the largest potential to be better than the best-known value while controlling the exploration versus exploitation trade-off. As a result, this figure is important to illustrate how BO makes efficient steps to select new samples to update the objective function [24].

Acquisition functions play a key role in BO, which involves determining how the exploration–exploitation trade-off is resolved [25]. These functions decide the next point to sample by estimating the improvement potential of the new sample solution over the best value found so far, taking into account the mean estimate and the variance of the surrogate model. Common acquisition functions include EI, probability of improvement (PI), and upper confidence bound (UCB). EI, for example, is defined as follows:

EI(x) = E[max(0,f(x)−f(x​+​))]

where f(x​+​) is the best-observed function value [26]. This work ensures that the areas with high potential improvement are selected, which means that there is always a way of symbolizing exploration of the unknown regions while still focusing on the promising regions.

19.2.2 Components of Bayesian Optimization

Surrogate Model: In the general context of the BO process, the surrogate model actually captures the function of interest. GP is used more often because it possesses a high degree of flexibility to approximate any arbitrary nonlinear function. GPs offer mean prediction of the given function along with an indication of the variability or uncertainty in that prediction, which is quantified by variance calculated using a probabilistic approach [27]. This double output enables BO to explore regions that the model assigns big standard deviations and exploit regions that the model assigns big means. In some cases, other models such as random forests or Bayesian neural networks can be used as surrogates depending on the nature of the problem or its dimensionality [28]. The choice of surrogate model plays a very crucial role in determining the efficiency and effectiveness of the optimization process that is undertaken in the BO [29].

Acquisition Function: Acquisition functions help in directing the optimization by indicating which points need to be evaluated next [30]. They are expected to work within the trade-off of exploration and exploitation to ensure that the search space is correctly explored as well as refined in promising areas [31]. The EI function, which most often serves as the acquisition function, is defined as the expected rise over the current best objective value, including both expected mean and variance [32]. PI centers on the likelihood that a point will enhance the current best solution by focusing on the most promising areas [33]. The UCB function combines the center of mass mean with the variability of the point’s variance by fixing a level of confidence and directs the search toward the space with the highest upper bound of the estimated value of the objective function [34]. All these functions are different in nature, and their use may depend on the nature of the optimization problem and whether more exploration or more exploitation is required.

19.2.3 Algorithmic steps

Algorithms involved in the BO process are described as follows: Firstly, one has to choose an approximate model, which is usually a GP, for the objective function. Several starting points are taken in order to overcome this and optimize this model – a small number of samples serve as a starting point for training [35]. The next step is to choose an acquisition function, whereby the choice will define the next point to be sampled. A specific acquisition function is then used to maximize this quantity to find a point that has the most potential for improvement based on the predicted value and the level of uncertainty [36].

Once the point is selected, the objective function is computed, and the calculated data is used to update the surrogate model and enhance the model's accuracy as well as prediction uncertainties. This means that the process of choosing a point with acquisition function to get its value in the true objective function and then updating the surrogate model is repeated [37]. The iterations proceed until the convergence, that is, when a predefined number of iterations are reached, the amount of time is elapsed, or the improvement in the results is less than a defined amount. Over these iterations, the BO appropriately seeks the parameter space, and this is particularly useful where the function assessments are strenuous. This systematic approach enables BO to provide approximate solutions in relatively fewer numbers of attempts, thus making it an efficient approach toward optimization for AI and machine learning.

19.3 Applications of Bayesian Optimization in AI

19.3.1 Hyperparameter Tuning in Machine Learning

Hyperparameter selection is one of the most crucial steps when it comes to machine learning model implementation because the selection of many parameters directly influences the model outcomes. Some of the regular methods used in hyperparameter tuning include the grid search and the random search methods, and these may prove to be time-consuming and costly, where large model situations are invoked. When compared to this, BO is a more efficient approach since it takes an organized approach to evaluate the variation in the hyperparameters and uses a model to estimate its performance. This also helps to explore the best regions of the hyperparameter space while helping the optimization process to converge over time, hence leading to better models being found. For example, consider a machine learning model with hyperparameters θ that need to be optimized to minimize a loss function L(θ). BO constructs a probabilistic model of L(θ), using a GP to estimate the EI over the best-known loss. Thus, through the constant sampling and updating of the surrogate model used in BO, the best hyperparameter values or settings that promote a low loss function can be identified easily, enabling improvement of the general performance of the model.

Figure 19.5 illustrates the experimental study of hyperparameter tuning for the convolutional neural network (CNN) in an autonomous driving problem using BO, random search, and grid search. The plot demonstrates the object detection model accuracy of successive iterations and how different methods increase accuracy while searching the hyperparameter space. Hence, BO proves to be much faster and provides a much higher level of increased accuracy in comparison to both random search and grid search, which underscores the usefulness of the algorithm in the choice of efficient hyperparameters. This figure demonstrates the use of BO on how it can be integrated to solve real-world problems, especially where the performance of models is key.

Figure 19.6 illustrates how the search space for the neural architecture is explored using BO. Here, the figure represents different neural network architectures comprising layers and units per layer, as well as the performance of different architectures. Some of the sampled points by BO are depicted to show how the method reaches high-performing architectures. The figure also captures what defines BO, namely the trade-off between exploration and exploitation, as it navigates through the architectural space for the best-performing architectures in terms of accuracy with respect to the validation set and computational complexity.

19.3.2 Neural Architecture Search (NAS)

Neural architecture search (NAS) is the procedure of determining likely structures of neural networks that would provide optimal performance based on defined goals. NAS can be a very large space, especially for more complicated structures; it may involve factors such as the number of layers, type of activation functions, or connectivity patterns. BO is critical to NAS because it serves as a systematic way to navigate the defined search space. Applying a response surface in parallel to reflect the performance of various architectures, BO leads the search toward the best-performing architectures. This approach is also effective in ensuring that, on the one hand, the organization is trying out new, risky, and rather unproven architectures, on the other hand, it is capitalizing on proven, promising architectures. For instance, parameters that constitute a given neural network’s architecture could include discrete and continuous constructs, while the technique of using BO involves the ability to maximizing an acquisition function that predicts the degree of improvement in performance. This approach to NAS enables one to strike a balance in arriving at the best-performing architecture faster and more economically.

19.3.3 Reinforcement learning

Reinforcement learning’s objective is to find a policy that yields the highest cumulative reward in an environment. It can also be observed that there is a close relationship between parameters such as learning rates, discount factors, exploration strategies, and the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms. Thus, with the help of BO, one can improve these parameters and the process of learning, leading to the acquisition of a better policy. In essence, the reward function is modeled as a black-box function whose properties are uncertain, and since BO relies on this surrogate model, the latter’s uncertainty guides the search process of the former. This is very useful, especially in reinforcement learning, as the reward signal can be virtually small and noisy. For instance, the optimization problem can be formulated in the context of the expected cumulative reward, R(θ), which is defined as the goal with regard to the parameter set θ. Through successive selection and evaluation of these parameters according to an acquisition function, BO ensures the discovery of settings optimal for policy learning, thereby enhancing the efficiency and performance of reinforcement learning techniques.

19.3.4 Automated Machine Learning (AutoML)

Automated machine learning (AutoML) is therefore the procedure of automating various aspects such as model selection, feature engineering, and hyperparameter tuning so that machine learning can be done by anyone. As mentioned, BO is one of the crucial parts of AutoML since it allows for a systematic search of the space of possible models and hyperparameters. In its deterministic nature, it assists the AutoML system in finding models and hyperparameters that are most likely to give good performance on a given dataset through the construction of a probabilistic model of the performance of different configurations. It also eliminates the time and human effort that would be needed to perform experiments manually while at the same time enhancing the quality of the generated models. For instance, in AutoML, BO can be applied for determining suitable algorithms, their hyperparameters, and preprocessing steps, thereby eliminating machine learning as a process. As a result of integrating BO into AutoML frameworks, it becomes easy to search through the large space of all model configurations, resulting in the creation of high-performing and resilient models with little to no human interference. As a result of utilizing BO, AutoML systems can be provided with the capability of reaching the level of performance, which is a state of the art in various tasks and domains, thereby proving the efficiency of BO in AI tasks.

19.4 Case Studies with Real-Time Applications

19.4.1 Case Study 1: Optimizing Hyperparameters for Deep Learning Models in Autonomous Driving

In studies of autonomous driving, object detection is one of the critical tasks, especially using CNNs. These models are used for real-time recognition and grouping of objects on the road, including pedestrians, vehicles, and traffic signs; therefore, it is extremely crucial that this model is very accurate. The goal of this case study is to enhance the detection models for objects in self-driving cars by increasing the efficiency of CNNs with adaptively set hyperparameters. BO is thus a commercialized technique that helps in hyperparameter tuning to find the best solution that optimizes the model while at the same time minimizing the cost of computations.

In this case, a BO approach is used to optimize parameters such as learning rate, batch size, the number of layers, and the filter sizes of CNNs. The GP helps in modeling the dependency of the detection accuracy upon the hyperparameter settings that BO selects during the process of navigating through the hyperparameter space. This is achieved through an acquisition function such as EI, which directs the selection of hyperparameters that are likely to produce higher accuracy. It tries out multiple configurations in order to identify those that are best suited and updates the surrogate model with this information. This approach clearly yields higher precision and recall rates than the models tuned using grid or random search methods. Furthermore, the results concern saving the processing time related to trained models, which is a key parameter when it comes to real-time applications such as self-driving cars, where quick decisions have to be made.

The plots represented in Figure 19.7 indicate how epoch-by-epoch object detection accuracy is enhanced for a CNN used in autonomous driving. The plot then analyzes the relative usefulness of BO compared to random search and grid search in fine-tuning the model’s parameters. The outcomes emphasize how this method of BO improves accuracy with more speed and efficiency compared to conventional optimization of hyperparameters. As shown in this figure, BO is effective in improving the quality of models in sensitive areas like autonomous driving, supporting the notion that the method has many real-world applications.

In a reinforcement learning scenario, Figure 19.8 depicts the cumulative reward observed over episodes while using BO, random search, and grid search. Hence, the figure depicts how tuning of parameters using BO leads to faster learning and better cumulative rewards. As the new efficient method of optimization, BO enables the reinforcement learning policy to make better decisions, thus enhancing robotic systems’ decision-making abilities. This figure shows how superior BO is in use cases that need fast learning or dynamic adjustment.

19.4.2 Case Study 2: Neural Architecture Search for Image Classification in Healthcare

In the diagnosis of diseases and medical conditions, medical image classification involving MRI scans and X-rays, among others, requires accurate and efficient methods. The purpose of this case is to find the specific topologies of neural networks where the classification of medical images will give high accuracy and where BO works well. NAS is a task of searching for the network architecture from the huge space of possible architectures, where one has to decide about the number of layers, types of connections, and forms of activation functions. BO helps in this search by modeling the probability of architectures’ performance and concentrating on compact architectures.

In this case study, BO is used for the automation of the search for corresponding neural network architectures for medical image classification. The process starts with the generation of the initial condition that defines the search space: the number of layers, the size of the filters used in the convolutional layers, the type of pooling operations, and so on. There is a probability distribution of the architecture’s accuracy provided by using a GP model, given only a few evaluations. It is applied to focus the search toward architectures where the acquisition estimate is high, indicating efficient pruning of the search space. The findings show that for medical image classification problems, BO is able to find architectures with superior accuracy compared to previously reported architectures at a considerably lower computational expense. These optimized architectures not only improve diagnostic efficacy but also reduce the training time of the model, making them very useful in clinical settings.

19.4.3 Case Study 3: Tuning Reinforcement Learning Parameters for Real-Time Decision-Making in Robotics

For instance, in industrial applications like assembling, welding, or the lifting of materials, robotic arms prove very useful since real-time decisions need to be made rapidly. Specifically, the aim of this case study is to improve decision-making scenarios for robotic arms in manufacturing applications using principles of reinforcement learning with an appropriate choice of parameters. Reinforcement learning deals with an agent’s ability to make decisions over time while trying to maximize cumulative reward, and the efficiency of these algorithms depends on factors including learning rate, discount factor, and the exploration-exploitation policy.

The use of such parameters needs to be tuned appropriately, and this is where BO offers a reliable means for fine-tuning reinforcement learning algorithms, so as to optimize the speed at which the robot can learn and/or make accurate decisions. Optimization precedes the parameter space identification that includes significant parameters influencing the policy learning of the robot. A meta-model, usually a GP, is built to evaluate the expected reward from different settings of the parameters. The acquisition function controls the exploration process, targeting configurations of the parameters with the highest potential for increasing the robot’s performance. Using the surrogate model to always update new data of evaluations, BO optimally narrows down parameter values, thereby improving learning efficiency.

The findings presented in this case study show that optimistic features enhance the effectiveness of the robot’s learning considerably, thus decreasing the time necessary to train it for the next tasks. Also, management achieves prognostic and prescriptive accuracy, owing to optimal parameters enhancing the efficiency of business processes and decreasing the rates of error in manufacturing processes. These results highlight the use of the BO technique in current decision-making systems due to the realistic adjustment of parameters used in reinforcement learning.

19.5 Results and Discussion

19.5.1 Summary of Findings

The case studies apply BO to machine learning and reinforcement learning problems and show dramatic enhancements in metrics such as accuracy and efficiency, as well as in decreasing computational costs. Focusing on hyperparameter tuning for deep learning models in autonomous driving, the BO resulted in significant increases in object detection accuracy, increasing the precision and recall ratio. The optimized models, as expected, showed higher accuracy in a shorter processing time, making them suitable for applications in self-driving cars. Applying BO in the search for neural architectures for image classification in healthcare, the model achieved high recognition accuracy in tasks related to medical image analysis, including MRI scans and X-rays. This approach drastically cut down the time consumption compared to other exhaustive search methods, hence enabling the implementation of complicated models in clinical practices. For example, when used in adjusting the parameters of reinforcement learning for robotic arms used in manufacturing, the stability and precision of the robots’ learning process and decision-making were enhanced due to improvements in speed and accuracy, hence increasing the manufacturing output and decreasing error margins. These results illustrate the ability of BO to specify vast potential enhancements in numerous related AI applications, making it a useful tool for researchers and investigators.

Figure 19.9 presents an aggregate of optimization from various case studies pertaining to different fields such as object detection, NAS, and reinforcement learning. Here, the figure is drawn in bar charts to visually represent the relative values of different KPIs, including accuracy, efficiency, and computational cost of BO, random search, and grid search. This graph undoubtedly proves and shows how effectively BO helps to achieve more accuracy and efficiency at a lower computational cost, which make us sure that how effectively BO can be used in any field of AI. It also shows the general versatility of BO for the optimization of expensive and nonlinear functions.

Figure 19.10 represents the comparison of the heaviness of computations and the quality of optimization between various optimization methods. With the help of a scatter plot, it is evident how BO is able to provide an optimal solution with the least amount of computational work. Nonetheless, random search and grid search are found to have either higher costs or produce lower quality solutions. For instance, the above figure clearly conveys the promise that BO brings in leveraging the results while incurring little computational overhead to optimize the execution of most AI models and systems.

19.5.2 Comparison with Traditional Methods

In comparison to the conventional approaches such as grid search and random search, BO has certain benefits connected to the efficiency of the search and the quality of the obtained results. Earlier approaches merely entail the systematic or random search of the hyperspace, which is inherently slow and resource-intensive, particularly when dealing with spaces of relatively high dimensionality. Some algorithms such as grid search demand that the model tests all possible values of all hyperparameters; hence, with an increase in the number of hyperparameters, the number of times the model is tested increases exponentially. Random search, while more efficient, is also a time-consuming process since the user needs to consider numerous evaluations to define the finest setting. On the other hand, BO deliberately searches hypothesized regions of the parameter space by building a stochastic model of the objective function and concentrating on the areas with the highest profitability. With this targeted approach, new promising configurations with a significantly lesser number of evaluations can be discovered, making it less computationally intensive and faster. In addition, because BO includes probability estimates of uncertainty and optimizes the exploration–exploitation ratio, the solutions yield more enhanced performance measures, evident in the experiments conducted in the case studies.

19.5.3 Challenges and Limitations

However, like any optimization technique, it is not without problems when applied to BO. As is the case with many “big data” tools, the two main difficulties concern scalability: the dimensionality of the data and the models used. Although the use of such structures, such as GPs or others, may add flexibility in updating the surrogate model for the optimization task, the computational cost of these processes increases noticeably with the space dimensionality. This limitation comes at the cost of time required and may affect the efficiency of BO, especially when dealing with many hyperparameters. Furthermore, the overall success of the BO technique is highly sensitive to the quality of the surrogate model used in the process. These issues raise the question of whether and when surrogates are good enough, and in case the surrogate model does not accurately approximate the underlying function, highly suboptimal solutions could be accepted. Another difficulty is the computational cost used for the evaluation of the acquisition function, which aims to maximize in each step to determine which point has to be evaluated next. This can be time-consuming, especially when decisions have to be made within a short time frame. Solving these issues is crucial to the enlargement of the scope of BO application in various tasks.

19.5.4 Future Directions

Potential areas for future research in BO are better techniques for surrogate modeling, better acquisition functions, and use of this optimization in new environments. Enhancing surrogate models to improve their performance in high-dimensional spaces is another area of focus with methods such as sparse GP-based methods and deep kernel learning, as some of the approaches to improve the same. These techniques aim to make the advantages of GPs credible and reliable without compromising the computing time. As an ongoing promising approach, the design of acquisition functions with a better balance between exploration and exploitation is another important development direction. There are, for example, multifidelity optimization methods, which allow one to work with information of different levels of detail at once and, thus, make the process more efficient. Furthermore, the application of BO with other optimizing algorithms, for example, evolutionary ones, would be another enhancement factor. It is also helpful to search for new applications of BO in domains such as NLP or energy and financial modeling to better define its possible applications. Thus, by addressing the current difficulties and exploring new prospects, BO should be able to develop further as an effective technique for the optimization of large partially unknown and/or computationally costly functions in AI and other fields.

19.6 Conclusion

BO has become one of the most important optimization techniques in AI because of its several benefits over classical techniques. This chapter has discussed the basic ideas of the proposed approach, its use with examples, and the way it positively impacts AI systems’ performance. Fundamentally, BO is good for settings where it takes a lot of resources to evaluate the performance of a given set of parameters because it uses statistical models such as GPs to make predictions. This characteristic to reach a balance in exploration and exploitation by implementing acquisition functions such as EI and PI enables BO to perform well in instances with large search spaces and thus obtain the solution in significantly fewer iterations. The real-world applications of BO used in this chapter from hyperparameter tuning in deep learning models for autonomous driving to NAS in healthcare, and reinforcement learning in robotics are evident from the following case studies. These applications have demonstrated gains in value measures, for example, in accuracy, learning rate, and compute, implying that the application of BO has the potential and capability to enhance the development of numerous advanced AI areas.

It is therefore imperative to note that the use of BO in AI goes beyond enhancing performance to encourage innovation and the development of new technologies. The time needed for optimizing large numbers of model parameters, which have highly nonlinear relationships between these parameters, is significantly reduced by the use of BO, thus opening up the opportunity for the development and application of more sophisticated AI systems in a range of industries. For instance, the enhancement of neural network architectures for medical image classification in the healthcare sector can greatly contribute to the precision of diagnosis, thereby enhancing the fulfillment of patients’ needs appropriately. Thus, in applications such as autonomous driving, the deep learning hyperparameters that have been optimized can provide increased reliability and safety of self-driving vehicles, contributing to the penetration of autonomous technologies. In robotics, optimization of reinforcement learning enhances decision-making insights to bring the integration of intelligent robots in manufacturing, logistics, and service industries to higher levels of productivity.

Apart from particular examples, BO makes a contribution to the general field of AI by helping the development of generally superior and more versatile models. This is especially valuable because it has the potential to successfully solve high-dimensional optimization problems and release new possibilities for research, so scientists and engineers can work with models that were earlier considered to be too costly in terms of computing. Therefore, the appearance of this kind of algorithm is a breakthrough that gives a possibility to investigate different models that were earlier considered to be too complex for high-dimensional optimization. As this capability also propels an exponential advancement in AI innovations and discoveries, it also helps to identify new solutions to old challenges. Moreover, these ideas of BO can be combined with other optimization algorithms to make use of each algorithm's properties while at the same time using the strong aspects of the other algorithms, thereby expanding the envelope for AI.

The use of BO also affects the remaining aspect of AI capability, namely equality of access. This makes BO accessible to individuals who are not experts in machine learning and AI; it expands its use in many areas of application such that everyone can benefit from machine learning and AI. Such democratization can be beneficial and encourages the general development of further inclusion of AI into as many organizations as possible. The place of BO in the growth of the field of AI cannot be understated, as it is set to define the next steps of the AI evolution as well as incremental advances in the field.

In conclusion, one must acknowledge that BO is a powerful and valuable tool in an AI engineer’s arsenal, as it provides a structured way of optimizing complex and expensive-to-evaluate functions. Applied in diverse contexts of AI, it proves its ability to boost model accuracy, optimize operations, and lower computational expenses. By overcoming the issue of scalability and further improving the model, as well as investigating new fields of application, BO will remain one of the fundamental tools, optimizing and contributing to the further development of AI and the creation of new, smart solutions. These reflections from this chapter emphasize the relevance of BO in the continuous endeavor of developing AI to solve the world’s challenges.
